ch01.note: The Shinsengumi, the 'Newly Selected Corps,' was a band of swordsmen the Tokugawa shogunate licensed to police Kyoto in the last turbulent years of its rule. Formed in 1863, it was commanded by Kondō Isami with Hijikata Toshizō as its vice-commander, and this novel is its story, seen through Hijikata. At the point the narrative opens, in 1857, the corps still lies six years in the future, and the two men are only friends from neighboring farm villages.

A ri was about 3.9 kilometers, two and a half miles, so the two villages lay within some twelve kilometers of each other. The distances Toshizō covers in this chapter — two and a half ri to Fuchū, two ri to Hachiōji — are a couple of hours' walking apiece.

Ansei was a Japanese era name; its fourth year is 1857 in the Western calendar. Years were still reckoned by such era names, changed on the accession of an emperor or after some inauspicious event. Toshizō was then twenty-two.

The hachijūhachiya, the eighty-eighth night counted from the first day of spring in the old calendar — about the first of May. A marker of the farming year, the traditional time of the last frost and of the tea-picking, it fixes the action at the very start of summer.

Under the Tokugawa order, dress and hairstyle were badges of inherited class. A farmer's son wore the plain sukobin style; the shaved pate and oiled topknot of the warrior were not his to assume. For Toshizō, a peasant, to dress his hair in imitation of a samurai's was a small, deliberate insolence — of a piece with his boast that he would be a samurai one day, which in the event he became.

The nanushi was a village headman, the lowest office of Tokugawa rural administration: a leading farmer, not a samurai, who gathered the land tax and kept order for the domain. Satō Hikogorō (1827–1902), headman of nearby Hino, was married to Toshizō's elder sister and kept a fencing hall of the Tennen Rishin-ryū, the school Kondō would head; it was there the two trained. He remained Toshizō's kinsman and patron for life.

The Kurayami Matsuri, the great festival of the Ōkunitama Shrine at Fuchū, is still held every year from late April into early May. Its name — kurayami, darkness — comes from its central rite, the night procession of the shrine's mikoshi, once carried through streets with every lamp put out so the deity might pass unseen. The festival and its darkened procession are historical; the licentious free-for-all Shiba describes is the novel's dramatization of the old sense that the god's night stood outside ordinary rule, and should not be taken as documented custom.

The old day was divided into twelve two-hour periods named for the zodiac animals. The hour of the Dog ran roughly from seven to nine in the evening; the hour of the Rat, which sounds later in the chapter to open the procession, fell around midnight.

ch01.anchor: the daughter of a great Shinshū temple
ch01.note: Jōdo Shinshū, the True Pure Land school, is the one branch of Japanese Buddhism whose clergy have always married and raised families, so that a temple could have a daughter and descend in a hereditary line. Its lay followers are the monto, the parishioners named here, who by custom addressed the priest's daughter with the honorific rendered 'the young lady.'

Ishida sanyaku was a real patent remedy of the Hijikata house, sold for broken bones and bruises. The family made and peddled it from the early eighteenth century until Japan's postwar drug law ended it in 1948; Toshizō truly did hawk it on foot across the provinces, in the manner of the Toyama medicine sellers, with several hundred customers on his books. It was compounded from a riverside weed, charred and ground to powder and taken down in hot sake. Its efficacy, described so vividly in the next paragraph, is the tradition's own claim; the hot sake may have done as much as the powder.

A leap forward to 1864, seven years past the scene at hand. In the Ikedaya Affair the Shinsengumi stormed an inn in Kyoto and cut down a gathering of anti-shogunal loyalists — the exploit that made the corps famous. The novel reaches it in its course; here Shiba names it only to vouch for the medicine.

ch01.anchor: all shogunal domain and temple-and-shrine land
ch01.note: The Tama country west of Edo was held in fief by no warrior lord: it was tenryō, land administered directly for the shogun, together with estates belonging to temples and shrines. Because no samurai household was seated there, the district had, as the narrator says, no warrior families and no women of rank — which is the whole engine of Toshizō's frustrated craving for a high-born woman.

Yobai, 'night-crawling,' was a real custom of the old farming villages: a young man would slip into a girl's room after dark, and if he was welcome the match might be owned to later. The trick of wetting the wooden shutter-track, so it slides without its usual squeal, belongs to that lore. Shiba presents Toshizō's use of it, here and at the temple, as something colder than courtship.

Norishige of Etchū Province (early fourteenth century) was one of the great swordsmiths, counted among the ten disciples of the master Masamune and working in the Sōshū manner. His blades are prized for a swirling grain in the steel that connoisseurs call matsukawa-hada, 'pine-bark skin,' which Shiba renders here as a seaweed grain. Genuine signed Norishige are very few, so the dagger is a startlingly precious thing to find on an unknown woman.

The Saruwatari were the hereditary chief priests of the Ōkunitama Shrine, documented from the fourteenth century, so the woman is no commoner but a daughter of Fuchū's first sacerdotal house. 'Junior Fourth Rank, Lower' (jushii-no-ge) was a grade in the ancient court hierarchy, and 'Lord of Sado' an honorary title carrying no real province — marks of standing conferred on such a priest. The sister, Osae, appears to be the novelist's invention; like the heroine Oyuki later in the book, she is not a documented person.

ch02.note: The tōshō-ke were the court nobility (kuge) ranked high enough to be admitted to the emperor’s presence in the palace. The Kujō, named a few lines on, were one of the five regent houses (sekke) from which the imperial court’s regents and chancellors were drawn, the very summit of that nobility; the shodaibu houses mentioned later were court families of a lesser grade. That a shogunal official should quietly place a well-connected young widow in such a house points to a real tactic of the failing bakufu: as the Kyoto court turned politically dangerous in these years, the shogunate planted eyes and ears among the noble households to watch it.

ch02.anchor: a hatamoto of the line since the Mikawa days
ch02.note: A hatamoto (‘bannerman’) was a direct retainer of the shogun, ranked high enough to have the right of audience with him — a samurai of the Tokugawa house itself, as distinct from the vassal of some provincial lord. To be a hatamoto of the Mikawa days was the proudest pedigree of all: it meant the family had served the Tokugawa from their home province of Mikawa, before ever they rose to rule Japan. The goren-chū, rendered here ‘the lady,’ was the formal principal wife of such a man.

ch02.anchor: a bannerman of the kobushin-gumi at eight hundred koku
ch02.note: A samurai’s standing was measured in koku, the yearly rice stipend attached to his house — one koku, about 180 litres, being reckoned roughly what a person ate in a year. Eight hundred koku was a comfortable hatamoto income. The kobushin-gumi was the roster onto which bannermen holding no active post were placed: they drew their stipend but bore no office, a respectable idleness.

ch02.anchor: a swordsman of the Kōgen Ittō-ryū
ch02.note: The Kōgen Ittō-ryū was a real school of swordsmanship of the Chichibu hills in Musashi, founded in 1776 by Henmi Tashirō Yoshitoshi; its name honors the founder’s claimed descent from the Minamoto (Genji) of Kai. As the narrator goes on to say, it was carried to fame by the master Hiruma Yohachi (died 1840), of Umehara in the Koma district, after whom his son Hanzō ran it from a head hall at Hachiōji — making it, along the Kōshū Highway, the direct rival of Kondō’s Tennen Rishin-ryū.

This paragraph sketches the pedigree of the school to which the novel’s heroes belong. The Tennen Rishin-ryū was founded in the late eighteenth century by Kondō Kuranosuke, a wandering swordsman of Enshū, and passed down not by blood but by adoption, each headship going to a promising pupil, often of farming stock. Its third head, Kondō Shūsuke (in retirement, Shūsai), adopted a Tama farmer’s son named Katsuta and renamed him Kondō — the Kondō Isami of this book, who would command the Shinsengumi. The school’s rough, close-quarter practicality, scorned in the polished halls of Edo, is a recurring note in the story.

ch02.anchor: the Ryūgō-ryū, based at Warabi in Bushū
ch02.note: The Ryūgō-ryū was a genuine martial school founded by Okada Sōemon (1765–1826), notorious for the low, shin-cutting attacks the narrator calls a ‘brawler’s fencing.’ It was a comprehensive art that taught the glaive (naginata) as well as the sword, which is why Toshizō’s shin-sweep, a page on, is said to carry ‘something of the glaive folded into it.’ Because a strike to the unarmored shin fell outside the polite conventions of the Edo halls, orthodox swordsmen disliked meeting it. Warabi lies just north of Edo, in what is now Saitama.

ch02.anchor: it might well be a Yasushige
ch02.note: Yasushige was a name borne by smiths of the Shitahara school of Musashi, near Hachiōji; an unsigned blade attributed to such a smith is a good weapon of uncertain authorship, judged by its workmanship rather than a signature. That it is a wazamono means a blade graded, in the old connoisseurs’ lists, for proven cutting power. Its length is given as two shaku four sun: a shaku is about 30.3 centimetres and a sun a tenth of that, so the blade runs some 73 centimetres, a full fighting sword. The ‘scent’ that rises from the steel is the misty temper-line along the edge that connoisseurs prize.

Under the Tokugawa order the public use of a surname was a privilege of the samurai and a few licensed commoners; an ordinary farmer went by his given name and his village alone. A prosperous old farming house like the Hijikata nonetheless kept its surname and used it in private — hence a ‘hidden’ surname, one Toshizō was not entitled to flaunt but was proud to own. That he announces it here, at the point of killing, is of a piece with the samurai topknot of the opening chapter.

ch02.anchor: the mokuroku of the Tennen Rishin-ryū
ch02.note: A fencing school certified a pupil’s progress by ranked licenses of transmission. The mokuroku was a middle grade, a catalogue of the techniques a student had been formally taught; above it lay the menkyo and, at the summit, kaiden, the ‘full transmission’ of the school’s secrets — the rank Nagakura Shinpachi is said to hold a little further on. To claim the mokuroku was to claim real standing, though not yet mastery.

Kondō’s hall in the Koishikawa district of Edo was the Tennen Rishin-ryū’s city base, kept up alongside the school’s country teaching out in Tama. Known to later history as the Shieikan, it was where the nucleus of the future Shinsengumi — Kondō, Hijikata, Okita, Inoue, and the rōnin house-guests named in this chapter — gathered in the years before 1863. A whole chapter to come is given over to it.

ch02.anchor: The Kantō officers are poking around Warabi
ch02.note: These were the men of the Kantō torishimari shutsuyaku, the shogunate’s roving rural police for the eight provinces of the Kantō plain, commonly called the hasshū-mawari, ‘the eight-province rounds.’ Because the Tama country and much of the Kantō was a patchwork of shogunal and temple land under no single lord, keeping order in the villages fell to these circuit officers rather than to any domain’s retainers.

Inoue Genzaburō (1829–1868) was a historical figure, from Hino like Hijikata and, like him, a man of the Tama circle around Kondō; he trained in the same Tennen Rishin-ryū. He followed the others to Kyoto and became captain of the Shinsengumi’s Sixth Unit, serving to the last: he was shot and killed in the Battle of Toba-Fushimi, the opening clash of the Boshin War. Here he is simply Kondō’s trusted man, sent to look into the killing.

Nagakura Shinpachi (1839–1915) was one of the finest swordsmen of the Shinsengumi and captain of its Second Unit. Son of a retainer of the Matsumae domain resident in Edo, he held the full transmission (kaiden) of the Shintō Munen-ryū. Unusually, he survived the wars of the Restoration by nearly half a century and left a memoir, a chief source for what is known of the corps from the inside.

Tōdō Heisuke (1844–1867) was another of these house-guests who became a Shinsengumi captain, of the Eighth Unit and the youngest of them. He trained in the Hokushin Ittō-ryū, the great Edo school of Chiba Shūsaku, then at the height of its fame. Heisuke later left the corps with Itō Kashitarō’s breakaway faction and was cut down by his old comrades in the Aburanokōji affair of 1867.

ch03.note: The meshimori-onna, literally ‘rice-serving women,’ were the maids that a post-town inn was licensed to keep — nominally to wait at table, in fact prostitutes. The shogunate tolerated them within limits (two per inn was a common legal ceiling, freely exceeded), as a lesser evil that kept the highway’s trade moving. Ojare was the local by-name for them here. They were indentured, poor, and, as the next paragraphs make plain, worked hard and briefly.

Chūgen: the lowest of a samurai household’s male servants, who carried sandals and spear and did the rough work — commoners in service, not warriors. That the school’s pupils ran to townsmen and footmen, not the sons of the bannermen next door, is the narrator’s way of marking how humble a concern the Tennen Rishin-ryū still was.

Okita Sōji (about 1842–1868), later the most gifted swordsman the Shinsengumi produced. A prodigy of the Tennen Rishin-ryū, he had trained at Kondō’s Edo hall from boyhood and would captain the corps’s First Unit and, briefly, head the school itself. He is a bright, boyish presence through much of this book; consumption killed him at Edo in 1868, before he was thirty, while his comrades fought on in the north.

The Hachiōji Sennin Dōshin (‘thousand foot-guardsmen’) were a real body, and a peculiar one: some thousand low-ranking warriors, largely remnants of the Takeda of Kai whom Ieyasu took into service, settled at Hachiōji to guard the western approaches to Edo — the Kōshū Highway and the Kobotoke Pass. Half-samurai and half-farmer, they held their land, drew a small stipend, and worked the fields between duties. Their presence made Hachiōji a town unusually full of men who bore swords, which is why the fencing schools of this chapter throve there.

Iai is the art of the sword drawn and cutting in one motion, from the sheath — the killing stroke delivered before the blade is even fully out, against an enemy at conversational distance. It is a different discipline from the give-and-take of a fencing bout, and a genuine iai master, able to kill from a seated bow or a moment’s stillness, was a specially dangerous man. Shichiri’s mastery of it, and Toshizō’s study of how to counter it, drive the rest of the chapter and the next.

ch03.anchor: the Nen-ryū at Maniwa in Jōshū
ch03.note: The Maniwa Nen-ryū, based at Maniwa in Kōzuke (Jōshū, present-day Gunma), is one of the oldest sword schools still transmitted in Japan, kept in the Higuchi family since the sixteenth century and long rooted among the farmer-warriors of that province. That Shichiri came up through it, before ever he took to the Kōgen Ittō-ryū, marks him as a serious and old-fashioned swordsman.

ch03.anchor: His iai was the Araki-ryū of Jōshū
ch03.note: The Araki-ryū was a composite martial tradition of Kōzuke that taught iai among much else and was known for showy drawing-feats. The anecdote of Ōshima Shingoemon (died 1779) catching over the roof a blade thrown for him is of that kind — the sort of trick-drawing (kyoku-nuki) prized as a display of control. Shiba offers it to gauge Shichiri’s pedigree; the point for Toshizō is that a man trained so can put a sword where it is not expected.

ch04.note: A famous piece of fencing lore. The Chiba house of Edo ran the Genbukan, one of the three great halls of the late shogunate, and taught the Hokushin Ittō-ryū founded by Chiba Shūsaku. His second son, Chiba Eijirō (1833–1862), was a prodigy nicknamed the ‘Little Tengu’ — a tengu being a mountain goblin of superhuman swordsmanship. The story is that, faced at a tournament with the Ryūgō-ryū’s baffling shin-cut, Eijirō sat and thought out the counter on the spot: not to snatch the leg forward, but to draw it back heel-first, so the mind need not dwell on the shin at all. The Owari Dainagon who hosts the tournament was the Tokugawa lord of Owari, one of the three senior branches of the shogunal house.

The waiwai-tennō were a real class of Edo-period mendicant — a kind of licensed beggar-priest who, dressed incongruously in haori, hakama, and two swords and wearing a long-nosed tengu or Sarutahiko mask, hawked cheap woodblock talismans of the Gozu Tennō from house to house, chanting and clamoring for coins. The Gozu Tennō (‘Ox-Head Heavenly King’) was the plague-warding deity of the Gion and Tennō shrines, and the charms were bought as a guard against summer pestilence. The point here is that the disguise let the Hachiōji swordsmen, masked and armed, loiter along the highway near Toshizō’s village without remark.

The Ansei Edo earthquake of 1855 leveled much of the shogunal capital and killed some tens of thousands. Coming two years after Perry’s black ships forced the country open, it was widely felt as an omen, and Shiba uses it here to date the general unease — earthquake, foreign crisis, and political ferment running together — against which the beggar-priests and their charms multiplied.

ch04.anchor: the clamor to expel the barbarians
ch04.note: Jōi, ‘expel the barbarian,’ was the cry that swept Japan after the American and European powers forced their treaties on the shogunate in the 1850s. Fused with sonnō, ‘revere the emperor,’ it became the slogan of the loyalist movement that would bring the Tokugawa down; the Shinsengumi, whose making this novel tells, were raised in good part to fight the men who raised that cry. Here it is only the distant noise of a world turning uneasy, still years from the events at its center.

ch05.note: A daikan (rendered ‘intendant’) was a shogunal officer who administered a district of the Tokugawa house’s own lands — collecting the tax, keeping the peace, judging suits — in place of a resident lord. Because the Tama country was such land, it answered not to a daimyō but to these officials, among them the Egawa house, hereditary intendants at Nirayama in Izu, a famous and capable line. Their light hand, the narrator argues, is why the district bred so many independent, sword-bearing farmers.
A chō was a measure of distance of about 109 metres, some 120 yards; thirty-six chō made one ri. Fifteen or sixteen chō is thus rather over a mile.

The Taiheiki (‘Chronicle of Great Peace’) is a sprawling fourteenth-century war-tale of the wars between the Northern and Southern Courts, long a staple of the professional storytellers; the Sangokushi that Okita names beside it is the Chinese Romance of the Three Kingdoms. That the variety-hall audiences had lately filled with samurai, and the reciters turned to battle-chronicles to suit them, is Shiba’s quiet index of a country drifting toward war.

A real battle, fought here in 1333 during the war that brought down the Kamakura shogunate. Nitta Yoshisada, risen for the emperor Go-Daigo against the ruling Hōjō, was checked at Bubaigawara by the Kamakura army, fell back to Horikane, and, reinforced overnight by Miura Yoshikatsu of Sagami, broke the shogunal host the next day and marched on to take Kamakura itself. (Shiba’s ‘southern side’ is a loose backward glance; the split of Northern and Southern Courts came a few years later.) The point for the chapter is the ground: a place shaped for battle, which Toshizō is about to read like a general.

The term is kuchi, taken from the ancient Chinese Art of War of Sunzi, which counts among its nine kinds of ground the one ‘where the highways of several states meet,’ a place from which one may command the movements of all. Toshizō, self-taught, applies the classic’s categories to a paddy-field crossing near his home village; the flourish is meant to show a natural strategist at work with a peasant’s materials.

ch06.anchor: the Kusunoki school, that traces itself to Kusunoki Masashige
ch06.note: Okita is teasing Toshizō by naming the two great traditions of Japanese military science (gungaku). The Kusunoki-ryū claimed descent from Kusunoki Masashige, the fourteenth-century commander famous for holding impossible positions by cunning against the odds; the Kōshū-ryū descended from the celebrated tactics of Takeda Shingen, the sixteenth-century warlord of Kai (Kōshū). To answer ‘the Hijikata school’ is Toshizō’s dry way of saying his generalship is his own invention — which, the novel insists, it is.

ch06.anchor: a shogunal foot-guardsman posted in Edo
ch06.note: The okachi were foot-samurai in direct shogunal service, a modest rank well below the mounted bannermen. Okita’s father held such a post in Edo — his family was formally attached to the Shirakawa domain in the north — so that Okita, though he passes as a masterless man, was a city child of the samurai class, which is why his tongue is so much quicker and more polished than the farm-bred Toshizō’s.

This is the famous tablet affair at the Ikaho shrine in Kōzuke. As the passage recounts, Chiba Shūsaku, the rising founder of the Hokushin Ittō-ryū, meant to hang at the shrine a votive tablet carved with his new pupils’ names; the old-established Nen-ryū of the province, seeing its following poached and its dignity slighted, mustered to stop him, and the two sides nearly came to a pitched battle before Shūsaku withdrew. The episode is genuine and well known. Shiba’s particulars differ from the documentary record, which puts the confrontation in 1823 (the sixth year of Bunsei, not the third given here) and names the Nen-ryū head as of the Higuchi family, not ‘Maniwa’ — Shiba takes the surname from Maniwa, the school’s seat. The parallel with the present feud, country school against country school, is the point.

ch07.anchor: Tsukahara Bokuden, Itō Ittōsai, Miyamoto Musashi
ch07.note: The legendary sword-saints of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries: Tsukahara Bokuden and Itō Ittōsai, founders of famous lines, and Miyamoto Musashi, the duelist-philosopher of The Book of Five Rings. Shiba’s point is not to belittle them but to mark a shift: the great late-shogunate halls had turned swordsmanship from a mystic personal Way into something teachable in bulk, by method, to thousands.

ch07.anchor: First, fighting spirit; second, fighting spirit
ch07.note: The word is kigumi: the marshalling of one’s whole spirit or will, brought to bear so as to overwhelm an opponent before technique is even joined. It was the watchword of the Tennen Rishin-ryū, whose strength lay less in polished form than in ferocity and nerve — excellent for a real killing, as the last chapters showed, but a liability in a points bout with the bamboo sword, which is the bind this chapter turns on.

ch07.anchor: one of the three great halls of Edo
ch07.note: The three great fencing halls of late-shogunate Edo were the Genbukan of Chiba Shūsaku (Hokushin Ittō-ryū), the Renpeikan of Saitō Yakurō (the Shintō Munen-ryū hall named here), and the Shigakukan of Momonoi Shunzō. A tag of the day summed them up: ‘the technique of Chiba, the rank of Momonoi, the power of Saitō.’ That Kondō’s obscure country school kept a quiet arrangement to borrow a ringer from so grand an establishment measures the gulf between them.

A momentous first entrance. Katsura Kogorō (1833–1877), of Chōshū, was at this time head student of Saitō Yakurō’s Renpeikan and a swordsman of the first rank; he would become, as Kido Takayoshi, one of the three chief architects of the Meiji Restoration that overthrew the shogunate. Here he is merely a hired stand-in earning pocket-money, and Toshizō — who will spend his life fighting men like him — meets him for the first time, seeing only a man born to every advantage he himself was denied.

Another of the age’s great names, dropped in passing. Sakamoto Ryōma (1836–1867), of Tosa, trained in the Hokushin Ittō-ryū at the Chiba hall in Okechō and would become the most famous go-between of the Restoration, brokering the alliance of Chōshū and Satsuma before his assassination. The tale of his scoring the deciding thrust on Katsura at a tournament is a popular one, told here as such.

Chōshū, the Mōri domain at the far western tip of Honshū, would within a few years become the fiercest engine of the anti-shogunal movement and the Shinsengumi’s great enemy — its loyalists the very men the corps was raised to hunt in Kyoto. The narrator is careful to note that in the year of this scene none of that has begun: the name means nothing to Toshizō yet, as he is not yet what he will become.

Harada Sanosuke (1840–1868), a house-guest here and later a captain of the Shinsengumi, from Iyo in Shikoku; a spearman by training and a famously hot-blooded, open-handed man. He fought with the corps through its Kyoto years and died in the fighting around Edo in 1868.

ch08.note: The Kōbusho was the shogunate’s own military academy, opened in Edo in 1856; its fencing hall drew up formal conventions for matches, and it is those the country school apes here — the measured nine paces, the bow, the best of three bouts. That Kondō’s obscure hall observes academy etiquette for a hired grudge-match is part of the chapter’s comedy.

ch08.anchor: sprang back into the low guard
ch08.note: The three basic guards named through this bout are the overhead (jōdan), the sword raised above the head to threaten a downward cut; the middle (chūdan), the point leveled at the opponent, the standard ready position; and the low (gedan), the point dropped, inviting an attack in order to counter it — hence its name as the ‘cunning’ or wary stance.

ch08.anchor: Tobari Fushigorō, a pupil of this hall
ch08.note: When a small hall could not field a swordsman good enough for an inter-school challenge, it would quietly hire a ringer from a stronger school and pass him off under a house name; ‘Tobari Fushigorō’ was the standing pseudonym Kondō’s hall used for such a borrowed man (the reading Fushigorō is the source’s own furigana). The joke is that the ringer here is Katsura Kogorō, one of the finest blades in Edo.

A famous stroke of foreshadowing. The historical Katsura (later Kido Takayoshi) was renowned for evading danger rather than meeting it — his enemies mocked him as ‘Runaway Kogorō,’ and his gift for slipping away kept him alive through the years when so many loyalist swordsmen were cut down. Where Toshizō lives by the blade, Katsura declines the contest and outlasts them all.

Harada’s scar was a point of pride and a standing anecdote of the corps: mocked once for being a mere townsman who could not properly disembowel himself, he is said to have cut his own belly on the spot to prove he could — and lived. The wound is the mark of the reckless, all-or-nothing temper the chapter goes on to describe.

ch09.note: Idaten (Skanda) is a swift-footed guardian deity of Buddhism, proverbial for speed; to call a man ‘an Idaten’ is to call him fleet as the wind. Okita’s teasing name for Toshizō sets up the chapter’s feat: the thirteen ri from Edo to Hachiōji run through in a single night.

ch09.anchor: the Day of the Ox in the dog-days
ch09.note: The doyō no ushi no hi, the Day of the Ox in the midsummer hot-season, was reckoned the most potent day of the year for gathering medicinal herbs (it is also the day the Japanese traditionally eat eel for stamina). The Hijikata family timed the harvest of their patent-medicine weed to it.

Dokudami (Houttuynia cordata) is a low, heart-leaved weed of damp shady ground, notorious for a strong, rank smell and long used in folk medicine. The detail of its crushed juice on Osen’s bare feet fixes the sordid physicality of the scene.

ch09.anchor: the warring days of Genki and Tenshō
ch09.note: The Genki and Tenshō eras (roughly 1570–1592) were the height of the Warring States, the age of Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi; to invoke them is to say that the old settled boundaries have broken down and men are seizing ground by naked force again.

ch10.anchor: beggar-monks of this sort had walked the provinces
ch10.note: The sutasuta-bōzu was a species of gannin-bōzu, a lay mendicant who performed pilgrimages, austerities, and prayers by proxy for a fee. Near-naked but for a straw rope and headband, beating time and chanting ‘sutasuta’ as he trotted, he was a familiar street-figure whose patter Harada mimics here; Shiba notes their revival in the unsettled last years of the shogunate.

The Hie (or Sannō) deity is the tutelary god of Mount Hiei, the great monastic mountain northeast of Kyoto; its shrines spread with the lands of Hiei’s Enryaku-ji temple. Shiba’s point is that a Kyoto-region god had been carried far east to the Bandō (Kantō) country to guard a temple estate — a small marker of how deep the old capital’s reach once ran.

Shiba gives the Hijikata a warrior pedigree drawn from old records (the Kamakura chronicle Azuma Kagami and a later gazetteer): a Minamoto man in the twelfth-century Genpei war, and in the Warring States one of a band of ten mounted local barons who served the Odawara Hōjō as leaders of military-farmer colonists. Whatever its exactness, it is the kind of descent many well-off Tama farming houses claimed, and it grounds the novel’s theme of farmers with the blood and temper of samurai.

In 1590 Tokugawa Ieyasu was transferred to the Kantō plain and made Edo his seat. The Tama country thereby became shogunal domain, its old warrior-farmers turned to peaceable agriculture to feed the swelling city — which is why, generations on, its people were farmers who still remembered how to fight.

ch10.anchor: the Aizu War and the Hakodate War
ch10.note: A leap forward to the novel’s end. In the Boshin War of 1868–69 the collapsing shogunate’s forces made their last stands in the northeast, at Aizu, and finally at Hakodate in Ezo (Hokkaidō), where Hijikata Toshizō would die. Shiba traces the guerrilla tactics of those campaigns back to the village brawling of the Tama country shown here.

A good blade: Fujiwara Yoshihiro was a name of the Hizen school of smiths (the line of Tadayoshi), esteemed in the Edo period. Its length, two shaku four sun, is about 73 cm — a full fighting sword hidden in a beggar-monk’s straw mat.

ch11.anchor: This year, the second of Bunkyū.
ch11.note: The Bunkyū era ran 1861–1864; its second year is 1862. From here the novel’s clock is the crowded calendar of the shogunate’s last years, and Shiba dates his chapters closely against it.

The measles epidemic of Bunkyū 2 (1862) is real and was catastrophic: the first outbreak in twenty-six years, it swept Edo through the summer, and contemporary tallies record on the order of seventy thousand deaths in the city, with far higher estimates. The Faroe detail is Shiba’s dramatization: the celebrated Faroe measles epidemic — studied by the Danish physician P. L. Panum, a landmark in epidemiology — was in 1846, not 1862. Sources: Panum, Observations… on the Faroe Islands in the Year 1846; Edo mortality records (Edo shichū hashika byōnin chōsho).

The Bukō Nenpyō (‘Chronological Tables of Edo’) is a year-by-year record of the city compiled by the Edo scholar Saitō Gesshin (1804–1878); it is a standard source for the daily texture and disasters of late-Edo life, and Shiba quotes its entries for the epidemic almost verbatim.

ch11.anchor: cut down outside the Sakurada Gate
ch11.note: The assassination of the great councilor (tairō) Ii Naosuke, Lord of Hikone, by Mito and Satsuma loyalists at the Sakurada Gate of Edo Castle on a snowy morning in the third month of 1860. Ii had pushed through the treaties opening the country and had purged his opponents; his murder shattered the shogunate’s prestige and opened the era of political killing this novel enters.

ch11.anchor: the Liangshan marsh in the Water Margin
ch11.note: The Water Margin (Chinese Shuihu zhuan, Japanese Suikoden) is the great Chinese novel of a band of a hundred and eight outlaws who gather at the Liangshan marsh; a byword, in Japan as in China, for a fellowship of brave and lawless men. The comparison casts Kondō’s hall of penniless swordsmen as just such a robbers’ roost.

Kiyokawa Hachirō (1830–1863), a rural samurai of Shōnai in Dewa and a Hokushin Ittō-ryū adept, is one of the pivotal schemers of these years. He talked the shogunate into raising the Rōshigumi — the corps that carries Kondō and Toshizō to Kyoto — meaning all along to turn it to the imperial cause, as the coming chapters show. He was assassinated by shogunal agents later in 1863.

ch11.anchor: a corps of masterless warriors at government expense
ch11.note: This is the Rōshigumi, the ‘corps of masterless men.’ Kiyokawa’s proposal — that the shogunate itself pay and arm the very rōnin who were terrorizing Kyoto, on the reasoning that poison is safest gathered in a box — is the hinge on which this whole novel turns: it is how a band of Tama farmers’ sons comes to Kyoto and becomes the Shinsengumi.

A senior councilor (rōjū) was one of the small group of daimyo who formed the shogunate’s governing cabinet. This is Itakura Katsukiyo (1823–1889), Lord of Matsuyama in Bitchū, who sanctioned the Rōshigumi and served the shogunate almost to its fall.

ch11.anchor: Saitō Hajime, a rōnin of Akashi in Banshū
ch11.note: Saitō Hajime (1844–1915), here a quiet house-guest of the Shieikan, would become captain of the Shinsengumi’s Third Unit and one of its most feared swordsmen. Almost alone among the leaders he survived the wars, serving afterward as a Meiji policeman and dying in old age.

ch11.anchor: a defector from the Sendai Date domain
ch11.note: Yamanami Keisuke (1833–1865), the learned house-guest whom Toshizō cannot abide. He would rise to be the corps’s general secretary, second in rank to Kondō; but as Shiba’s parenthesis warns, the very gentleness of nature shown here would destroy him — in 1865, having tried to leave the Shinsengumi, he was made to commit seppuku.

ch11.anchor: today's student leagues at Tōdai and Waseda
ch11.note: One of Shiba’s deliberate modern asides (the novel was serialized in 1962–64). He likens the mixing of hot-headed young men from every domain at the great Edo fencing halls to the militant student movements (the Zengakuren) then convulsing Japan’s universities — a comparison meant to make the reader of his own day feel the political ferment.

ch12.note: Shiba presents the man Toshizō visits as a collateral Tokugawa of the line of Tadanaga (the disgraced younger brother of the third shogun, Iemitsu): grand in pedigree, slender in stipend, and of a rank that would never, in a settled age, have received a masterless swordsman. That he does receive them is Shiba’s measure of how far the old order had already loosened.

ch12.anchor: Kondō's one beloved book was Rai San'yō's Nihon Gaishi
ch12.note: The Nihon Gaishi (‘Unofficial History of Japan,’ completed 1827) by the Confucian scholar Rai San’yō is a stirring, imperial-centered narrative of the rise and fall of the warrior houses. Enormously popular, it did as much as any book to shape the loyalist sentiment of these years; that the plain-minded Kondō reads it and weeps over its heroes tells us exactly where his heart lies.

Kondō’s attachment to a blade by the great Edo smith Nagasone Kotetsu is famous — and famously misplaced. By the best accounts his ‘Kotetsu’ was a forgery: a blade by the brilliant contemporary smith Minamoto Kiyomaro carrying a faked Kotetsu signature. Saitō Hajime later said he had bought it cheap at a secondhand shop in Yotsuya because it looked the part, and that Kondō, knowing it false, treasured it all the same. The whole episode rhymes with Toshizō’s own hunt for a signature in this chapter.

Here the novel turns romance. The ‘Nosada’ is the second-generation Kanesada of Mino (Muromachi period), so called because he cut the 定 of his signature in a variant form read no-sada; his blades rank among the very sharpest ever forged. But the sword the historical Hijikata actually carried through his life was not this Muromachi masterpiece bought from a blind Asakusa dealer — that scene is Shiba’s invention. It was a blade by the eleventh-generation Aizu Kanesada, a smith of Hijikata’s own day, and it came to him in Kyoto, a gift connected to the Aizu lord Matsudaira Katamori. Source: records of the surviving Hijikata Kanesada and the Aizu Kanesada line.

Wazamono (‘sharp blades’) is a formal ranking of swords by cutting power, drawn up in the Edo period from the tests of the Yamada family of official sword-testers; the top grade is the ‘great’ wazamono. The Izumi-no-kami Kanesada stands among its most highly rated names. (Shiba gives the count of top smiths as twenty-one; the published lists vary.)

A grisly relic of the Warring States. Mori Nagayoshi (1558–1584), a ferocious general under Nobunaga and Hideyoshi called the ‘Demon Musashi,’ is said to have carried a cross-bladed spear made by this Kanesada, on which he graved the words Ningen Mukotsu, ‘man without bones’ — his boast that flesh gave his blade no more resistance than a boneless thing. The Hosokawa lords named just before, Yūsai and his son Tadaoki, were great cultivated daimyo of the same age.

Tsujigiri, ‘crossroads-cutting’: cutting down a random passerby in the dark, whether to rob him, to test a new blade, or merely to blood oneself. Long a capital offense, it flared up again in the murderous, masterless mood of these years, and Toshizō, we see, goes out hunting the hunters.

ch12.anchor: the sixty-eight stages of the Nakasendō
ch12.note: The Nakasendō was the great inland highway from Edo to Kyoto, threading the central mountains through sixty-nine post-stations (Shiba counts the stages between them); slower and steeper than the coastal Tōkaidō, but without its unbridged rivers. A hundred and thirty ri is roughly five hundred kilometers, a march of some ten or twelve days.

ch13.note: Mibu, then a village of temples and farms in the western outskirts of Kyoto, became the first base of the corps that grew into the Shinsengumi; the men were mocked by the townsfolk as the Mibu-rō, the ‘Mibu wolves.’ The Yagi and Maekawa houses that quartered them still stand as sites of the corps’s history.

In the Heian capital the Suzaku Ōji was the great central boulevard running south from the palace, some eighty-odd meters wide; by the nineteenth century its line lay out among the western fields, and Mibu’s ‘antique grace’ is the ghost of that vanished grandeur.

Mibuna, a leafy green of the mustard family developed around Mibu itself, milder and more tender than its relative mizuna; pickled, it is a Kyoto specialty. Yamanami’s rapture over it, and Toshizō’s refusal to touch it, make a small comic emblem of the gulf between the two men.

The Tengu-tō was the radical revere-the-Emperor faction of the Mito domain, which in 1864 would rise in open rebellion and be crushed with great bloodshed. Serizawa’s claim to have belonged to it marks him as a man of the most violent loyalist stripe.

ch13.anchor: Serizawa Kamo was a rōnin who had left the Mito domain
ch13.note: Serizawa Kamo (1826/27–1863), a huge, drunken, dangerous Mito rōnin of the Shindō Munen-ryū. His real name is given variously (the source’s Kimura Tsugiji is one form); he had genuine ties to the Mito radicals. As co-commander of the founding Mibu corps he would prove so violent and disgraceful that Kondō and Toshizō — his allies here — assassinated him within the year. Source: standard Shinsengumi histories; the identification of his names is itself disputed.

Matsudaira Katamori (1836–1893), Lord of Aizu, who in 1862 was made Kyoto Protector (Kyoto Shugoshoku), the shogunate’s chief authority in the capital. It is under his patronage that the Mibu corps will be taken up and become the Shinsengumi — which is exactly the connection Toshizō is scheming toward here, through Serizawa’s Mito kinsman. (‘Lieutenant-General,’ chūjō, renders his court title.)

Sonnō jōi, ‘revere the Emperor, expel the barbarian’ — the slogan that fused loyalty to the throne with hatred of the foreigner into the age’s great revolutionary cry. Kiyokawa’s stroke is to reveal that the shogunate’s own hired corps is to serve it, turning the shogun’s guardsmen into the Emperor’s vanguard.

The Emperor Kōmei (reigned 1846–1867), whose extraordinary dread of foreigners made him a natural, if reluctant, figurehead for the expel-the-barbarian cause; his opposition to the treaties gave the loyalists an imperial authority to set against the shogunate’s policy.

ch13.anchor: grow into a man past recognizing
ch13.note: The young shogunal overseer here, Yamaoka Tetsutarō, is the future Yamaoka Tesshū (1836–1888): swordsman, calligrapher, and Zen adept, who in 1868 would ride alone into the imperial army’s camp to arrange the peaceful surrender of Edo. Shiba’s aside marks how green he still is, taken in by Kiyokawa like all the rest.

ch13.anchor: the Akechi Mitsuhide of the theater
ch13.note: Akechi Mitsuhide is the archetypal traitor of the Japanese stage: the general who turned on his lord Oda Nobunaga and destroyed him at the Honnō-ji in 1582, only to fall days later. For Serizawa to see Kiyokawa as ‘an Akechi’ is to brand him a betrayer of his master — here, the shogunate.

ch13.anchor: the greatest bold stroke of theater
ch13.note: Kiyokawa’s gambit did not last. Alarmed, the shogunate ordered the Rōshigumi back to Edo within weeks; most obeyed, and Kiyokawa was cut down there by shogunal agents in the fourth month of 1863. But a small remnant refused to leave Kyoto — Kondō’s Tama men and Serizawa’s Mito men — and stayed on under Aizu’s protection. From that remnant the Shinsengumi was born, which is why Shiba lingers on this night at the Shintoku-ji.

ch14.anchor: —To spend one's loyalty to the last, and requite the nation.
ch14.note: The four-character motto jinchū hōkoku (尽忠報国), “serve the nation in perfect loyalty.” Its locus classicus is the Chinese History of the Song, where the words are said to have been tattooed on the back of the loyalist general Yue Fei; among the Mito school of imperial loyalism, from which Serizawa came, it had become a watchword.

ch14.anchor: the Aizu Middle Captain Matsudaira Katamori
ch14.note: “Middle Captain” renders chūjō, a senior rank in the court’s Palace Guards. Matsudaira Katamori, lord of Aizu and Kyoto Protector (see the glossary), held it, and is often named simply the Aizu Chūjō.

Newly opened in 1863, and not to be confused with the modern peers’ school: a hall within the Imperial Palace where the ablest court nobles were set to study policy toward the shogunate. In practice it became a channel through which the loyalist rōnin who frequented it pressed their program on a court with, as Shiba says, no political training of its own.

ch14.anchor: Sasaki Tadasaburō, a shogunal retainer and instructor at the Kōbusho
ch14.note: A shogunal swordsman (1833–1868). The narrator’s parenthesis runs ahead of the story: within weeks Sasaki’s party would indeed cut Kiyokawa down in Edo. The same Sasaki is generally held to have led the assassination of Sakamoto Ryōma four years later.

Kiyokawa Hachirō was killed on the thirteenth day of the fourth month of Bunkyū 3 (30 May 1863). Scholarship places the spot at Azabu Ichinohashi; Shiba writes Akabanebashi, a neighboring bridge in the same Shiba–Azabu quarter of Edo. The discrepancy of place is left standing and noted; the killing itself, by Sasaki Tadasaburō’s men, is well attested.

The killing, on 14 September 1862, of the English merchant Charles Lennox Richardson, cut down by Satsuma retainers when he failed to give way to Shimazu Hisamitsu’s procession at Namamugi village on the Tōkaidō. Britain’s demand for redress led, in August 1863, to the naval bombardment of Kagoshima, the Anglo-Satsuma War. Shiba’s account of the affair is accurate.

See the glossary. The name means the “Newly Levied Corps” — a near-twin, in sound and sense, of the Shinsengumi that the breakaway men at Mibu would take, and a reminder that the two bodies sprang from the one rōnin levy.

“Newly Selected Corps.” Shiba grants the name here, at the spring break with Kiyokawa, through the Aizu liaison. Historically it is usually dated some months later, after the coup of the eighteenth day of the eighth month of 1863, and the record is divided over who bestowed it — the court–shogunate liaison nobles (the Buke Tensō) or Matsudaira Katamori of Aizu. The novel telescopes the chronology; the men, and the Aizu patronage, are as given.

Bunkyū 3, third month, thirteenth day, falls on 2 May 1863 — the founding moment of the Shinsengumi, which would be destroyed with the shogunate five years on. The corps’s stay in Kyoto under Kiyokawa had lasted, as the text says, some twenty days.

ch14.anchor: The matter of the letter K
ch14.note: In the original the Aizu man names Kiyokawa only as ki-moji, “the ki letter” — the first sound of the name, uttered so as never to speak it whole. Rendered here as “the letter K.”

ch15.note: A jibe the townsfolk made on Mibu-rō (壬生浪, “the Mibu rōnin,” itself a pun on the “Mibu wolves”). By a slight shift of sound it becomes mi-boro (身ぼろ), “tattered of body” — rags, the lot of them — a mock at the corps’s threadbare state.
Imo-dōjō: a “sweet-potato” or bumpkin’s hall. The sweet potato being humble country fare, the name mocked Kondō’s Shieikan in Edo as a poor, rustic school without the polish of the great city halls.
The ryō was the chief gold unit of the Tokugawa coinage. Sums of five or seven, set against the tens of thousands of koku a domain drew, measure how far a private band of rōnin stood below a lord.
See the glossary. Kyoto’s licensed pleasure quarter; with Gion it is the scene of much of the corps’s off-duty life, and, in Serizawa’s case, of its disgrace.

ch15.anchor: These he gave the name jokin
ch15.note: Toshizō’s officer scheme, modeled on Western company organization, is historical. Above the line-officer jokin the corps-captains were styled kyokuchō (commander), with fukuchō (vice-commander) below; the internal watch were the kansatsu (inspectors). By keeping the vice-commander’s post and the inspectors in his own hand, Hijikata — as the text says — held the working machinery of the corps while leaving Kondō the title.

The Kōnoike were the greatest merchant-and-banking house of Osaka, lenders to daimyo and shogunate alike; their name stood for money itself. That housebreakers should be at their Kyoto premises marks the disorder the new corps was set to check.
A genuine record, the diary of the Aizu official Hirosawa Tomijirō. Shiba quotes it to show how the corps struck a contemporary eye — not as police, but as a thing to be feared and looked away from.
A practice sword of split bamboo bound in leather, used with padded armor for full-speed bouts; the standard weapon of the Edo fencing halls, and the reason a “pass” could be fought without blood.

ch16.anchor: a zasshō, a low retainer in a noble's service
ch16.note: A zasshō was a lay steward or man-at-arms in the household of a court noble — in older days an aozamurai, a “green” or low-ranking samurai. The great houses, defenseless in a violent age, had lately been hiring men who could use a sword.

A goyōkiki (or meakashi): a townsman licensed to inform and make arrests for the authorities, badge of office the iron truncheon (jitte) he here keeps hidden. In Edo such men swaggered; in loyalist-ridden Kyoto they went in fear.

“Bunkichi the Monkey,” a Kyoto police-informer who hunted loyalists for the shogunate. In the intercalary eighth month of 1862 the Tosa loyalists killed him and hung his body, naked, at the Sanjō riverbed. The episode is historical; the riverbed at Sanjō and at Shijō was the loyalists’ place for displaying such “punishments” (tenchū).

Agents of the Kujō house on the shogunal side, both killed in the loyalist terror of 1862. Shimada was cut down by Satsuma men, in the first of the “Heaven’s-punishment” assassinations that swept Kyoto that year; Shiba’s account of the house’s fright is borne out by the record.

See the glossary. The distinction matters: the Shoshidai was the regular shogunal government of Kyoto, concerned with law and evidence, whereas the Shinsengumi, Toshizō insists, existed only to use the sword.

Tuberculosis. Okita Sōji’s cough, first noted here, is the illness that will take him young, off the battlefield, a few years on; the recurring beat of the cough shadows him through the rest of the book.

A work-song of the winter fields of Toshizō and Okita’s home country, sung while treading down the young barley. Hearing it drift from the restaurant tells Okita, and the reader, that a Bushū man is among the party inside.
See the glossary for the canal itself. Its banks, lined with the domains’ mansions and their armed men, made this stretch the most dangerous ground in Kyoto for two lone corpsmen to walk.

ch17.note: The Urabon or Obon, the Buddhist festival of the dead kept in the seventh lunar month, when the ancestral spirits are welcomed home with lanterns and chanting and the nenbutsu, the invocation of Amida Buddha. To Toshizō, bred to the plainer country Bon of Bushū, the Kyoto festival’s incense-heavy piety is merely oppressive.

ch17.anchor: the long poem on the Honnō-ji
ch17.note: Rai San’yō’s celebrated poem on Akechi Mitsuhide, the general who in 1582 turned on his lord Oda Nobunaga and destroyed him at the Honnō-ji. The line Kondō has copied marks the fork where Mitsuhide, ostensibly marching west toward Bitchū, wheeled instead on the capital — the moment of his unspoken resolve, remembered as “the enemy is at the Honnō-ji.” Reading it, Toshizō turns the phrase inward: the corps’s real enemy is not Chōshū but Serizawa, within.
Burei-uchi: the samurai’s customary right to cut down a commoner for an insult. Serizawa’s abuse of it, killing for trifles, is among the misdeeds that mark him for removal.

The Kiheitai, the “irregular militia” raised in Chōshū in 1863 by Takasugi Shinsaku, open to commoners as well as samurai and drilled in Western arms — a sharp break with the old warrior monopoly on soldiering. That Akazawa was a Kiheitai man of Shimonoseki townsman stock, no hereditary retainer, is why his loyalty sat so loosely.

Historical. On the twelfth of the eighth month of 1863 Serizawa, refused a “loan” by the rich Kyoto silk-merchant Yamatoya Shōbei — who had bankrolled the loyalist Tenchūgumi — brought his men back that night and burned the storehouses to the ground. The arson, close by the Imperial Palace, outraged the court and hastened Serizawa’s own end.
For a stray tea-stalk to float upright in the bowl was reckoned a small omen of good fortune — the maid’s cheerful reading, against which Toshizō’s black thought is set.

A tayū was a courtesan of the first rank, the accomplished and costly summit of the Shimabara quarter, versed in music, verse, and games. To be received by one, and to have her send old poems after him, marks Toshizō as more than a common guest.
About eight in the morning. The old day ran in twelve two-hour periods named for the zodiac animals; the hour of the Dragon (tatsu no koku) fell roughly from seven to nine.

A celebrated Kyoto swordsmith of about 1600. That Toshizō’s short-sword should be a Kunihiro, paired with his Izumi-no-kami Kanesada long sword, is of a piece with the book’s steady care for the blades its men carry.

ch18.note: Kaishaku: at a seppuku, the man who stands behind and strikes off the head to end the suffering once the belly is cut. For Toshizō to name himself Niimi’s second — and with the very sword of the man Niimi had murdered — is at once a mercy and a verdict.

ch18.anchor: held up to the warrior's code, has nothing to be ashamed of
ch18.note: The chapter’s argument turns on shidō, the “way of the warrior” (see the glossary). Serizawa presses the orthodox view, that a warrior’s code has meaning only in service to a lord; Kondō and Toshizō, masterless farmers’ sons, make the code itself their lord. From this grows the corps’s written code and the machinery of enforced suicide by which Toshizō will rule the Shinsengumi.

Shidō fukakugo, “a failure of resolve in the warrior’s code” — the formula under which the corps ordered a man to die. Vague enough to cover almost anything, it became the standing charge of the Shinsengumi’s internal justice; Niimi is its first victim in the book, Noguchi its second, in the same year.

The warriors of the Kantō plain (Bandō, “east of the passes”) in the age of the Genji and Heike wars, a byword for hardihood and plain fighting virtue. Kondō and Toshizō, of that same eastern farming country, take these old warriors, not the soft hereditary samurai of the Edo peace, for their model of the warrior.

A chūgen: the lowest grade of military servant, not a samurai at all, hired by the season to carry a lord’s gear. Harada’s rise from such a place, and the belly-scar of an old, half-botched suicide, set his rough loyalty apart from Serizawa’s born arrogance.
The character Kondō brushes is sa (左), the first of “Sanosuke” — Harada Sanosuke, whom he will not name aloud: a fifth man for the killing.

ch18.anchor: the eighteenth day of the ninth month
ch18.note: The night, in 1863 (30 October by the Western calendar), on which the Kondō faction killed Serizawa Kamo and Hirayama Gorō in the Yagi house, along with Serizawa’s mistress Oume. The deed is historical and was given out at the time as the work of Chōshū; which corpsmen actually struck is disputed in the sources, and Shiba’s roster is one account among several.

ch18.anchor: late in the hour of the Dragon
ch18.note: The source names the hour of the Dragon, which fell in the morning; but the scene is plainly night — “after sundown” above, “half past twelve” below — so an evening hour is meant. The slip is the source’s, and is left as it stands.

ch19.note: Toshizō really did keep haiku, in secret, under the pen-name Hōgyoku (“abundant jewel”). Forty-one of his verses survive in a booklet he compiled himself, the Hōgyoku hokku-shū, put together in the early spring of 1863, just before the Shieikan men went up to Kyōto; it is kept today at the Hijikata Toshizō Museum in Hino. The verses Shiba quotes in this chapter are drawn from it. By common account Hijikata was an earnest amateur and no better, which is the whole joke of the scene. Corroborated.

ch19.anchor: Natsume Seibi of Asakusa in Edo and the nun Matsubara-an Seifu
ch19.note: Both were real poets of standing. Natsume Seibi (1749–1817), a wealthy Asakusa money-changer, ranked among the leading haiku masters of his day and was an early patron of Kobayashi Issa. Matsubara-an Seifu (1732–1814) was a woman poet of a notable Hachiōji house who studied under Chōsui and then Shirao and took the hermitage-name Matsubara-an in its second generation. That Toshizō’s grandfather kept their company places the Hijikata, farmers though they were, among the cultivated houses of the Tama country. Corroborated.

ch19.anchor: by the law of that day, a disabled man could not inherit
ch19.note: Under Tokugawa house-law the headship and property of a family passed undivided to a single heir, and a son with a disqualifying disability could be set aside—here the blind eldest son, Tamesaburō, in favor of the second son, Kiroku. The hereditary given name Hayato went with the headship, not with birth order.

Gidayū: the dramatic chanting that carries the story in the puppet theater, sung to the shamisen. To be master of it “beyond a gentleman-amateur’s skill” is a serious accomplishment, not a parlor trick.

ch19.anchor: a black kite, a paper kite
ch19.note: A pun the English can only gesture at. The verse ends tobi, tako: tobi is the black kite, the hawk that wheels over Japanese towns, and tako the paper kite flown at the New Year—two “kites,” one bird and one toy, hanging together in the holiday sky. Okita laughs at the cheap wordplay.

The takashimada, a tall, formal dressing of the shimada coiffure, worn by young unmarried women and, at its most elaborate, by a bride. On a woman in samurai-style dress it reads as respectable and unwed—part of what makes Osae’s changed circumstances hard for Toshizō to place.

ch19.anchor: the Princess Kazunomiya's marriage down to the shogun
ch19.note: The political fault-line of these years. In 1861 the shogunate married Princess Kazunomiya, half-sister of the Emperor Kōmei, to the young Shōgun Iemochi, to bind court and camp together—the policy called kōbu-gattai, “union of court and shogunate.” The regent Kujō Hisatada (1798–1871) pushed the match through and was reviled by the loyalists as a shogun’s creature; in 1862 he was driven from office, made to take the tonsure, and retired to the Kujō lands south of the city. Osae serves this fallen house. Corroborated.

ch19.anchor: hereditary scholars of the National Learning
ch19.note: Kokugaku, the “National Learning”: an eighteenth-century movement to recover an ancient, native Japanese spirit from the oldest texts, against the imported learning of China. By the 1860s its emperor-centered strain fed straight into the loyalist, expel-the-barbarian politics Toshizō suspects in Osae; a hereditary kokugaku house in a court noble’s service is, to him, a house on the wrong side.

ch19.anchor: hasn't a tail sprouted somewhere on you
ch19.note: Toshizō’s teasing runs on the old belief in the shape-shifting fox (kitsune), which takes the form of a beautiful woman to deceive men and is betrayed by the tail it cannot quite hide; a bewitching creature of that kind is a bakemono, the “monster” Okita has just warned him Kyōto is full of. The joke carries a real fear: he cannot tell whether the Osae before him is his old lover or a lure.

ch19.anchor: the Matsuzakaya, a draper's in Ueno in Edo
ch19.note: The Matsuzakaya was one of the great Edo dry-goods houses; the draper’s where the boy Toshizō was placed is the direct ancestor of the department-store chain that still bears the name. That a Tama farmer’s son served a stint as an apprentice shop-boy in the city, and was sent home in disgrace, belongs to the received life of Hijikata.

ch20.anchor: once the country retreat of the abbess-princess of the Hōkyō-ji
ch20.note: The Hōkyō-ji was a real imperial convent whose abbesses were imperial princesses (see the glossary). Such convents kept country retreats (sato-gobō) away from the cloister; the one here stood “behind the Great Buddha,” the district around the colossal Buddha of the Hōkō-ji in Higashiyama. The institution and the geography are real; that this particular retreat served as a safehouse for masterless loyalist samurai, managed by Osae under cover of teaching poetry, is the novelist’s device. Institutions corroborated.

Ohaguro, the lacquer-blackening of the teeth, and the shaving of the eyebrows mentioned just before, were the marks of a married woman in this period; a wife blackened her teeth and plucked or shaved her brows. On the palanquin-master’s wife they are simply the badge of a matron.
The kan (or kanme) was a unit of weight of about 3.75 kilograms, so the water-filled cask ran to some 65 kilograms—the weight of a grown man, which is the point of loading it so.

ch20.anchor: a yotsude-kago; in Kyoto they call it a yotsuji-kago
ch20.note: A hired town palanquin of the plainest sort, an open litter with a hanging screen. Shiba notes a real dialect split: yotsude-kago (“four-hand palanquin”) in Edo, yotsuji-kago (“four-way palanquin”) in Kyōto and the Kamigata.

ch21.anchor: the tranquility of the Forbidden Interior
ch21.note: The kinketsu, the “forbidden gate” or Forbidden Interior: the Emperor’s palace in Kyōto. Kondō’s speech casts the corps’s street-killing as the guarding of the imperial peace.

ch21.anchor: its edict for the control of rōnin
ch21.note: Historical. In the twelfth month of 1863 the shogunate ordered the seizure or killing of unlicensed rōnin in the Kyōto–Osaka region, clearing the ground before the young Shōgun Iemochi’s second entry into Kyōto early in 1864. It is this licence to kill on sight that turns the Shinsengumi loose on the city. Corroborated.

ch21.anchor: a warring-provinces warrior of the Genki and Tenshō years
ch21.note: The Bandō musha were the eastern warriors of the medieval age; the Genki (1570–1573) and Tenshō (1573–1592) years fall in the Warring Provinces period, the age of Nobunaga and Hideyoshi. Toshizō’s “true samurai” is the fighting man of those centuries, before, as he sees it, the heritable stipend and the long Tokugawa peace softened the class.

ch21.anchor: was Kondō's staff, and not his line
ch21.note: Shiba reaches openly for the modern vocabulary of management—“staff” and “line”—to describe Toshizō’s maneuver: he kicks the learned, resented Yamanami upstairs into the grand-sounding post of general secretary (sōchō), nominally above the vice-commander, while stripping it of any power of command. Yamanami Keisuke really did hold the title of general secretary; his slow ruin, and his seppuku in 1865, are still to come.

ch21.anchor: The law is enough in three
ch21.note: An allusion to the hō-sanshō, the “three-article law.” On taking the Qin capital in 206 BCE, Liu Bang, founder of the Han, is said to have swept away the old cruel code and promised the people a law of just three articles. Okita’s guess that it was “one of the Tang generals” is the joke: he has the story from a variety-hall storyteller and has the dynasty wrong.

ch21.anchor: Working into the dead of night, five articles were made
ch21.note: The famous five-article Code of the Shinsengumi. Its historicity is not so solid as its fame. The name kyōkuchū hatto and the five-article form come chiefly from Shimozawa Kan’s Shinsengumi shimatsuki (1928); the survivor Nagakura Shinpachi records only four prohibitions, under the plainer name “interdictions,” and no contemporary document of the code survives. The fifth article and the celebrated title may well be Shimozawa’s crystallizing. What is firmly attested is the substance Shiba dramatizes: a discipline enforced to the death, by ordered seppuku, for cowardice and desertion. Provenance debated; the practice corroborated.

Sakai Hyōgo, a headquarters officer of the corps, was hunted down for desertion and killed near Osaka; the episode is preserved in the traditional Shinsengumi accounts. Those accounts, however, place his flight in 1865, after General Secretary Yamanami’s own seppuku, whereas Shiba brings it forward here to serve as the new code’s first test. The killing is attested; the timing is the novelist’s.

ch22.note: The era-name changed from Bunkyū to Genji early in 1864; the first year of Genji is 1864. The first day of the sixth month by the old lunar calendar fell on 4 July, and the Ikedaya raid four nights later on 8 July.

ch22.anchor: an Ōharame had passed along Kawaramachi
ch22.note: The ōharame were women from Ōhara, north of Kyōto, who carried firewood and charcoal-logs (kuroki) into the city on their heads to sell, in a dress of their own with white leggings. Their sing-song cry was a fixture of the Kyōto street.

ch22.anchor: the mimed Kumasaka Chōhan of the Mibu mystery plays
ch22.note: The Mibu kyōgen are wordless Buddhist morality-plays mimed to gong and drum at the Mibu-dera, near the corps’s own barracks. Kumasaka Chōhan is the giant robber of medieval legend, killed while raiding an inn; in the mime he lumbers about in an outsized mask. Okita’s private joke is that the harder the dreaded Toshizō scowls, the more he looks like that comic ogre.

The coup of the eighteenth day of the eighth month, 1863 (the third year of Bunkyū). Satsuma and Aizu, backing the moderates at court, drove the radical Chōshū faction out of Kyōto overnight; seven Chōshū-aligned court nobles fled with them to the west in the “flight of the seven nobles.” It is this humiliation that the Chōshū plotters of the Ikedaya mean to reverse. Corroborated.

ch22.anchor: the disguise assumed by Furutaka Shuntarō
ch22.note: Historical. Furutaka Shuntarō (1829–1864), a rural samurai of Ōmi and a shrine-retainer of the Bishamon-dō monzeki (an imperial-abbot temple), ran an arms depot in Kyōto under the merchant name Masuya Kiemon, supplying the plot to fire the city and carry the Emperor off to Chōshū. His seizure is the hinge of the whole affair. Corroborated.

ch22.anchor: suffered torture past the power of words, but in the end confessed nothing
ch22.note: Here Shiba takes a deliberate line on a disputed point. The famous tradition, which comes down from the early Shinsengumi chroniclers, has Furutaka broken under brutal torture at the Mibu barracks — hung upside down with a spike through his feet — and made to confess the fire-and-abduction plot, which then triggered the raid. Shiba instead has him hold out and gives the credit to the covenant-roster (renpanjō) seized at the shop, by which the conspirators’ names were already known. The seizure and killing are certain; how much the raid owed to torture as against captured documents is what the accounts dispute.

ch22.anchor: The storming of the Ikedaya was at the Hour of the Boar
ch22.note: The Ikedaya Incident, the night of the fifth day of the sixth month, Genji 1 — 8 July 1864. A handful of Shinsengumi under Kondō surprised a war-council of Chōshū, Tosa, and other loyalists at the inn and, after a two-hour fight, killed or took some dozens of them for the loss of few of their own. The raid broke the planned rising, made the Shinsengumi’s name across the country, and hardened the road to the Chōshū war that followed within the month. Corroborated.

ch22.anchor: in a letter Kondō sent to his adoptive father Shūsai in Edo
ch22.note: The passages that follow are quoted from Kondō Isami’s own letters to his adoptive father Kondō Shūsai, real documents in the stiff epistolary Japanese of the day; Shiba’s bracketed insertions (“passage omitted,” the gloss on the hours, “my adopted son”) are his. They are among the closest first-hand records of the fight, and their boasting tone is Kondō’s.

ch22.anchor: a hemp haori bearing the light-blue mountain-stripe
ch22.note: The Shinsengumi’s notorious uniform: a light-blue (asagi) hemp overcoat with a jagged “mountain-stripe” (dandara) hem, worn here over a leather fencing-cuirass, a mail undershirt, and an iron brow-guard. Shiba’s closing detail is a relic’s: the very brow-guard Toshizō wore, with two sword-cuts in it, was preserved in the Hijikata family house at Ishida in Hino. Corroborated.

ch23.anchor: A frontage of three and a half ken
ch23.note: The ken was a length of about 1.8 meters and the shaku about 30 centimeters, so the inn ran some 6.3 meters across the front and 27 deep, and the stair-corridor upstairs (below) a bare 90 centimeters wide — the narrowness that let a handful of men hold it. Shiba’s parenthesis is a modern traveler’s: the Ikedaya was pulled down in 1931 and a concrete inn stood on the site when he wrote.

ch23.anchor: the soba shop in the case of the Akō rōnin
ch23.note: The forty-seven rōnin of Akō, heroes of the most famous vendetta in Japanese history, are remembered as mustering at a soba (buckwheat-noodle) shop near their target on the night of their raid in 1703. Shiba likens the Gion meeting-house, where the corps put on its armor, to that staging-point.

Katsura Kogorō is the later Kido Takayoshi (see the glossary), one of the architects of the Restoration; the passages quoted are from his own diary. His being away from the Ikedaya when the corps struck is historical, and of a piece with a career of hairbreadth escapes that earned him the by-name “Kogorō the bolter.”

ch23.anchor: half of these would likely have held high office in the Restoration government
ch23.note: The roster is historical, and Shiba’s claim is sober rather than rhetorical. Yoshida Toshimaro, dead at twenty-four, was among the ablest pupils of Yoshida Shōin, the Chōshū teacher whose students went on to lead the Restoration; Miyabe Teizō was the senior Higo strategist of the cause. The raid is often said to have set the loyalist movement back by years by cutting down such men. Corroborated.

Kondō’s prized blade, a Nagasone Kotetsu (see the glossary). He wrote home that it came through the night’s fighting unbent while his men’s swords broke; whether his Kotetsu was a true work of that much-forged smith or one of the many fakes has been argued ever since.

Tamamushi Sadayū (1823–1869), a Sendai clansman who had crossed the Pacific with the 1860 embassy to the United States, kept in his Kanbu Tsūki a running record of the doings of court, shogunate, and clans; it is a standard source for these years. The figures that follow are his.

ch23.anchor: The dead on the spot on the men-of-purpose side were seven
ch23.note: The tallies differ across the sources: the loyalist dead are variously given as seven, eight, or nine on the night, with more dying later of wounds, and the captured at some twenty to twenty-three. Shiba follows one set of figures; the exact count was disputed from the first, both sides having reason to shade it.

ch24.note: In the shogun’s own capital, arrests fell to the yoriki and their dōshin — mounted and foot constables under the town magistrate. They were direct shogunal subordinates, yet hereditary petty officials, ranked with the gokenin (low retainers without the right of audience before the shogun) and shut out of the field service that was a warrior’s honor. Because their work handled blood, corpses, and the execution ground, warrior society counted it ritually polluting and scorned them as “defiling officials.” To offer Kondō — who styled himself a loyalist swordsman — the rank of “senior yoriki” was to file the Shinsengumi under police rather than soldiers, and that is the slight that galls him here.

Lord of Kuwana and, from 1864, Kyoto Shoshidai (the deputy who governed the capital under the Protector). He and the Kyoto Protector, Matsudaira Katamori of Aizu, were brothers, both sons of the Takasu house, so the two great security offices of Kyoto sat in one family. With Hitotsubashi Yoshinobu (ch. 28) they formed the shogunal-loyalist party later nicknamed the “Ichi-Kai-Sō.”

An obsolete bronze muzzle-loader: powder and a solid iron ball were rammed home, the ball first heated red so as to set fire to whatever it struck, and touched off with a match-cord — a heated-shot field piece with a range, as Shiba says, of barely a chō (about 110 meters). The “Nirayama guns” Toshizō covets were another order of thing: modern cast cannon from the reverberatory furnace raised at Nirayama in Izu by the intendant Egawa Tarōzaemon, one of the first Western-style ordnance foundries in Japan.

In shōgi, Japanese chess, the gyoku or king is the piece a player must protect above all others; once it is taken the game is lost. Kondō casts the Emperor as that king-piece — the one counter neither side can afford to have captured — which is precisely the logic of the war now opening: whoever holds the sovereign is in the right.

Two monuments of loyalist history-writing: the Dai Nihon-shi (“History of Great Japan”), the vast chronicle begun in the seventeenth century under the Mito branch of the Tokugawa, and Rai San’yō’s Nihon Gaishi (“Unofficial History of Japan,” 1827). Both held that legitimacy descended through the imperial line, and from them came the maxim Shiba cites — that the side which holds the Emperor is by definition the kangun, the imperial army, its opponents rebels. It is why Chōshū and the shogunate alike strained to seize the sovereign’s person.

Maki Izumi (Yasuomi), 1813–1864, a Shinto priest of Kurume and the most uncompromising theorist-strategist of the revere-the-Emperor, expel-the-barbarian cause, and a chief planner of Chōshū’s advance on Kyoto. When it failed he made his last stand on Tennōzan and died there by his own hand with sixteen companions (ch. 25).

ch24.anchor: the Hamaguri Gate of the palace
ch24.note: The Hamaguri-gomon, the “Clam Gate,” one of the gates in the wall that enclosed the Kyoto Imperial Palace. By tradition it was so named because, like a clam that opens only in fire, it had once been forced open by a great blaze after standing shut for years. The battle about to be fought at it gave the affair its lasting name: the Hamaguri Gate Incident (Kinmon no Hen) of 1864.

ch25.note: Marishiten (Sanskrit Mārīci), a Buddhist deity of light and the heat-haze, taken up in Japan as a guardian of warriors and invoked for victory and for the power to vanish from an enemy’s sight. Fighting men carried her image and prayed to her before battle, which is why Kanryūsai’s flattery lands where it does.

The Shinsengumi’s famous standard: the single character makoto (誌), “sincerity” or “fidelity,” in white on a red field. The same character marked the sleeve-bands of the corps’s pale-blue coats. It is the emblem by which the Shinsengumi is remembered.

The Mimawarigumi (“patrol corps”) was the respectable twin of the Shinsengumi: a mounted police force raised from the sons of hatamoto and put under the Kyoto Protector, where the Shinsengumi was a band of commoners and rōnin. Its commander Sasaki Tadasaburō and his men would later be held responsible for the killing of Sakamoto Ryōma.

ch25.anchor: Smite the Aizu Traitors, the Satsuma Rebels
ch25.note: Chōshū carried two standards: the loyalist watchword “Revere the Emperor, Expel the Barbarian” and, beneath it, “Smite the Aizu Traitors and the Satsuma Rebels” (tō-Kai-kan Sasu-zoku). The second named the enemies Chōshū blamed for its expulsion from Kyoto in the coup of the eighth month, 1863: Aizu, which held the city, and Satsuma, then allied with it.

This is the great fire that Kyoto remembered as the Dondon-yaki (also “the gun-fire burning”). Set off by the fighting of the nineteenth to the twenty-first of the seventh month, 1864, it swept the heart of the city and is reckoned to have burned on the order of twenty-eight thousand houses — a catastrophe far outrunning the battle that started it.

ch26.note: Itō Kashitarō (1835–1867) is the figure whose coming reshapes the middle of the book. A polished swordsman and a fluent theorist of the revere-the-Emperor, topple-the-shogunate school, he enters the Shinsengumi meaning to capture it from within — the design he lays out to Tōdō in this chapter. Three years on, the split he seeds here will end at the Aburanokōji: Kondō will have him killed and use his corpse to bait and cut down his followers.

ch26.anchor: the kinoe-ne of the first year of Genji
ch26.note: In the old sexagenary calendar every year bears one of sixty combined signs; kinoe-ne (甲子) is the first of the sixty, a year reckoned auspicious for new beginnings. Its two characters can be read kasshi as well, and from them the man took his new name, Kashitarō — announcing, in effect, a fresh start. The first year of Genji was 1864.

The Hokushin Ittō-ryū, founded by Chiba Shūsaku (1793–1856) at his Genbukan dōjō at Otamagaike in Kanda, was one of the three great fencing schools of late-Tokugawa Edo. Patronized by the loyalist Mito house, it turned out an extraordinary run of revolutionary swordsmen — Kiyokawa Hachirō, Sakamoto Ryōma, and others — which is precisely the political taint Toshizō smells on it.

Kinchō: a warrior sealed an inviolable promise by striking steel on steel — the guard of his own sword, or two blades together — so that the ring of the metal stood witness to the oath. Here Itō pledges to keep Tōdō’s murderous secret, without yet pledging the deed.

Takeda Kōunsai (1803–1865), an elder councillor of the Mito domain and leader of its radical loyalists. In 1864 he headed the armed rising of the Tengu Party (the “Tengu-tō”); it was crushed, and he was executed. That Itō stood close to such a man marks how far his own loyalism ran.

ch27.anchor: at the head of the Chōshū expedition
ch27.note: The punitive campaign the shogunate raised against Chōshū after the Hamaguri Gate affair had branded the domain a court enemy. This first Chōshū expedition, mounted in the winter of 1864, ended almost without fighting when Chōshū, its radicals for the moment beaten down, made a show of submission. Kondō’s errand to Edo is to urge the shogun to lead it in person.

Historically true. Through its minister Léon Roches, the shogunate sought French money and arms to fund the Chōshū war and to remodel its forces on the Western pattern. The scheme came, as Shiba says, to nothing, but it shows how near to bankruptcy the Tokugawa treasury had run — the point of Kondō’s whole boast.

“The eighty thousand horse of the hatamoto” was the proverbial fighting strength of the shogun’s direct bannermen. By the 1860s the figure was hollow: generations of peace on fat stipends had unmade the class as soldiers, so that Kondō can dismiss them as “straw dolls.”

Shinohara casts the conspiracy as a play. A “thousand-ryō actor” (senryō yakusha) was a top-billed kabuki star; a “ham actor” (daikon) the reverse; and the hanamichi, the “flower-way,” is the raised runway through the audience by which an actor makes his entrances. His warning is that Itō, the lone star of a cast of hams, may overact and tumble off the runway.

Two famous retainers of the twelfth-century hero Minamoto no Yoshitsune — the warrior-monk Benkei and Ise Saburō Yoshimori — bywords for brawny, ferocious fighting men. Okita is joking that Itō’s rough companions look the part.

ch28.anchor: In Kyoto, no doubt, they called make-up hotogara
ch28.note: Hotogara was a Bakumatsu word for a photographic likeness, and for the sitting that produced it. Toshizō, who has never heard it, takes it for a word for face-paint — which is the joke, for Kondō is indeed painted white: the wet collodion plates of the day were so slow that a sitter had to be powdered with lead-white and backed by white cloth, and to hold stone-still for a long exposure, to register at all.

ch28.anchor: Hitotsubashi Yoshinobu — the future fifteenth shogun
ch28.note: Tokugawa (Hitotsubashi) Yoshinobu, 1837–1913, then Superintendent of the Defense of the Imperial Palace and the strong man of the shogunal party in Kyoto. In 1866 he became the fifteenth and last shogun, and in 1867 surrendered the government to the Emperor. Shiba’s parenthesis looks ahead to that.

Ueno Hikoma (1838–1904), one of the first professional photographers in Japan, who learned the chemistry of the art at Nagasaki from the Dutch naval surgeon Pompe van Meerdervoort (the “Pompe” here) and kept a celebrated studio there. Many of the faces of the Restoration — Sakamoto Ryōma among them — survive only in his plates.

Matsumoto Ryōjun (1832–1907), a leading Dutch-school physician and the shogun’s own doctor, who studied under Pompe at Nagasaki. He grew close to the Shinsengumi in its last years and tended the consumptive Okita. After the Restoration, renamed Jun, he rose to Surgeon-General of the imperial army and was made a baron.
