ch28.anchor: an expel-the-barbarian man of the National-Learning school
ch28.note: The National Learning (kokugaku) was the nativist scholarship that sought Japan’s pure origins in its oldest texts and shrines, before any Chinese or Western taint. Its more fervent adherents held a “divine-land” faith that reckoned anything foreign a pollution — even a barbarian’s footprint, even a photograph — which is why Itō’s men will not so much as look at the camera.

The chapter ends on the fact. Yamanami, the learned senior man shelved as general secretary and drawn toward Itō, fled the corps in the second month of Keiō 1 (1865). Under the Code he himself had helped frame, desertion meant death: he was brought back and made to cut his belly, with Okita for his second. He was the most famous man the Code destroyed.

ch29.note: Chiba Shūsaku (1792/94–1855) founded the Hokushin Ittō-ryū and, in Edo, the Genbukan, one of the three great sword halls of the day (see ch07). Because the Chiba line stood close to the Mito Tokugawa, the school became a nursery of the domain’s revere-the-Emperor zeal — which is Shiba’s point here: Yamanami came up through it, and his politics came with it.

ch29.anchor: put to death at Tsuruga in Echizen
ch29.note: The Mito Tengu Party (Tengu-tō), the domain’s radical revere-the-Emperor faction, had risen in arms at Mount Tsukuba in 1864 (see ch13). Under Takeda Kōunsai (1803–1865), a former chief councillor of Mito, the survivors marched west to lay their case before Hitotsubashi Yoshinobu in Kyoto and, worn out, surrendered to the Kaga domain late in 1864. The junior councillor Tanuma Genba-no-kami then took charge, stripped and caged the prisoners in Tsuruga’s herring warehouses, and had them beheaded early in 1865: the dead numbered about three hundred and fifty (Shiba’s three hundred and fifty-two; some accounts give three hundred and fifty-three), Kōunsai and his family among them. The standard histories of the Mito rebellion corroborate the event, and reckon the butchery a turning point that swung radical opinion from ‘expel the barbarian’ toward bringing the shogunate down — exactly the shift Shiba marks in this chapter.

Beien, ‘rice and salt’, is a set phrase for the bare means of living; the Shinsengumi drew its keep from the shogunate. Yamanami’s revulsion is at eating the bread of the power that had just slaughtered men of his own persuasion.

ch29.anchor: hail fell about one sun across
ch29.note: A sun is an old unit of about three centimeters, a little over an inch; hail that size is a tall tale of the northern winters — the harmless, homesick sort of boast a doomed man falls back on when he will not speak of what waits for him.

ch29.anchor: A courtesan of Shimabara named Akesato
ch29.note: The scene that follows — the woman at the lattice, the small feet — is among the most famous in Shinsengumi lore, but it rests on a single late source, the popular chronicler Shimozawa Kan, and no register of the Shimabara quarter records a courtesan of this name in these years. Many historians doubt that Akesato existed at all. Shiba, writing a novel, keeps the cherished tradition; the reader should hold it as legend, not record.

ch29.anchor: the black-lacquered fair-weather clogs and the white tabi
ch29.note: Hiyori-geta are low lacquered clogs on shallow teeth, worn on fine days (the name means ‘fair-weather clogs’); tabi are the split-toed cloth socks worn with them. That Okita takes in only the footwear — not the weeping face he will not raise his eyes to — is how the passage carries the weight of what he is about to do.

ch30.anchor: take supreme command of the Second Chōshū Expedition
ch30.note: The first expedition of 1864 (see ch27) had ended almost without fighting when Chōshū feigned submission and beheaded three of its elders. This second expedition, decreed in 1865, was another matter: the domain had swung back to its radicals and rearmed, and, as Shiba says, the shogunate had neither the money, the strength, nor a lawful pretext for it. The Shogun Iemochi came up to command it in person, fell ill at Osaka Castle, and died there in 1866 as the campaign went against him — the war that broke the Tokugawa. The account is historically accurate.

The uma-jirushi was the tall battle-standard that marked a commander’s place in the field. The golden fan had been the Tokugawa house’s device since Ieyasu; to see it carried into Kyōto was to see the shogun come in war-array, which is why the townsmen read it as a show of power restored.

ch30.anchor: the kind of sacred palanquin was different
ch30.note: The whole knot of the age in one image. Kondō and Itō both revere Kusunoki Masashige (see ch12), the model of the loyal vassal — but Kondō’s loyalty runs to the shogun and Itō’s to the Emperor, so the same hero is borne, as it were, in two different palanquins. Toshizō sees that men on the same side already march under opposed flags.

Napoleon III, emperor of the French, backed the shogunate through his minister Léon Roches with loans and arms and a scheme to remodel its forces on the French pattern (see ch27). Shiba’s aside looks ahead: this same emperor would be captured at Sedan in 1870 and his throne fall, so that the shogunate had staked its revival on a patron about to lose his own. The forward glance is accurate.

The secret compact by which Satsuma and Chōshū, until then at each other’s throats, agreed to make common cause against the shogunate. Brokered by the Tosa men Sakamoto Ryōma and Nakaoka Shintarō, it was sealed at Kyōto early in 1866, joining Saigō Takamori of Satsuma and Kido Takayoshi — the Katsura Kogorō of this book — of Chōshū. It is the hinge on which the Restoration turns, and, as Shiba stresses, the Shinsengumi, whose whole business was to police Kyōto for the shogunate, never suspected it. (Ryōma’s band, the Kaientai from 1867, was at this date still his Nagasaki company, the Kameyama Shachū; Shiba uses the later name.)

ch30.anchor: the French system of army organization
ch30.note: The corps was recast on Western lines: the old rank of jokin (roughly, officer) was dropped, and ten numbered units under captains put in its place, in imitation of the shogunate’s newly French-drilled infantry. The new post of staff officer (sanbō) given to Itō was, like Yamanami’s old ‘general secretary,’ a grand title with no troops under it. Toshizō kept the real command as vice-commander, and had drawn the whole roster to seat Itō’s faction where it could do least harm.

ch30.anchor: and I'd fain drink long (Chōshū) and deep.
ch30.note: A street lampoon (rakushu) built on two puns the parentheses gloss: kyatsu, ‘that fellow,’ for Aizu, the domain then holding Kyōto, and nagashi, ‘long,’ for Chōshū. The conceit is a wife-swap — cast off the Aizu spouse, take a better, and drink deep with Chōshū — and it measures how the capital’s sympathy had turned from the shogunate’s enforcers toward the beaten domain.

ch30.anchor: Hurrying toward home, the clouds of the Fifth Month.
ch30.note: The joke Okita catches: satsuki-gumo, ‘clouds of the Fifth Month,’ is a summer season-word (kigo), yet Toshizō writes it in the eleventh month, deep in autumn. He would sooner have the bright summer word than a lonely autumn one — a small window, as Okita sees, onto the homesick heart beneath the cold enforcer. Toshizō signs his verse Hōgyoku (see ch19).

Nagai Naomune (1816–1891), a senior shogunal official; here Grand Inspector (ōmetsuke), the office set to watch the daimyō. Late in 1865 he led an embassy to Hiroshima to interrogate Chōshū over the coming war, and Kondō, Itō, and two others rode in his train — Kondō under the borrowed name Kondō Kuranosuke. The mission is historical; the Chōshū side, as Shiba says, sent a stand-in envoy and never meant to treat.

ch31.anchor: went also by the name of Fudōdō-mura
ch31.note: The corps’s grandest and last barracks, at Fudōdō-mura by Shichijō-Horikawa, a walled compound with a drill-ground, said to have housed some two hundred men. Historically the Shinsengumi did not move there until 1867 (before that they were billeted at the Nishi-Honganji); Shiba brings the move forward to set this night here.

The Kōnoike were the richest merchant-bankers of Osaka, lenders to daimyō and shogunate alike (see ch15). Self-styled loyalist rōnin preyed on such houses with forced ‘war-chest’ loans; to be rid of them the Kōnoike paid the Shinsengumi for protection, and the money went, as Shiba notes with some dryness, into Kondō’s pleasures. It is a small clear picture of how the corps was kept.

Ōtani Yoshitsugu (1559–1600), Hideyoshi’s able and much-loved general, later a stalwart of the losing side at Sekigahara. A famous anecdote has Hideyoshi say that he should like to give Ōtani a hundred thousand men and watch him wield them — the highest praise for a commander’s grip on a great army. For the Aizu officer to reach for it in speaking of Toshizō is to rank his generalship above Kondō’s.

ch32.note: The Totsukawa-gō was a mountain district of Yamato (modern Nara) whose gōshi, or rural samurai, held in return for old service a rare exemption from tax and a fierce, hereditary loyalty to the Emperor. Many came up to Kyōto as the Restoration neared — Totsukawa men had risen with the Tenchūgumi in 1863 — which is why one of them stands here among Shichiri’s hired swords.

Tanaka Mitsuaki (1843–1939), a Tosa loyalist who after the Restoration rose to count and Imperial Household Minister and made himself the great collector of the Restoration men’s records. Shiba breaks his own narrative to quote Tanaka’s recollection — the enemy’s own testimony to how the mere sight of Hijikata scattered the young loyalists — a real memoir set down in old age, long after the event.

A gandō was a hand-lantern with its candle hung in gimbals inside a hooded metal barrel, so that it stayed lit at any angle and threw its beam one way only, like a bull’s-eye lamp — the night-fighter’s and the housebreaker’s light.

ch32.anchor: the left-mitsudomoe crest on Toshizō's right sleeve
ch32.note: The mitsudomoe is a whirl of three comma-shapes, an old and common device; the ‘left’ form turns one way, the ‘right’ the other. This left-mitsudomoe was the Hijikata family crest. That the dead husband’s clothes Oyuki later brings out bear the very same crest is the quiet omen Shiba sets at their meeting.

None of this is history. Oyuki is Shiba’s one wholly invented character; in his afterword he says he made her up, to give Toshizō a private life the record does not supply, and so a door into the man’s inward self. The circumstantial detail — the art-name Kōka, the surviving paintings, the teacher Yoshida Ryōdō, the Ōgaki husband — is the novelist’s craft, not fact: there was no historical Oyuki. She recurs to the end of the book.

ch33.anchor: the fleet of four nations in the Bakan Strait
ch33.note: In 1863 Chōshū, obeying the Court’s order to expel the barbarian, had fired on foreign ships passing the Shimonoseki (Bakan) Strait. The reply came in the eighth month of 1864, when a combined fleet of Britain, France, the United States, and the Netherlands bombarded and stormed the Shimonoseki batteries and reduced them to ruin. It was the one time a single domain made war on the Western powers alone, and Itō turns it here to Chōshū’s credit. Historically accurate.

ch33.anchor: a direct retainer of the shogun's house
ch33.note: To be made a jikisan was to become a direct retainer of the shogun — a hatamoto or lesser bannerman of the Tokugawa house itself (see ch02), not the vassal of some provincial lord. The wooing begun here bore fruit: in 1867 the Shinsengumi was in fact raised as a body into the shogunate’s direct service, and Kondō given the standing of a hatamoto. For a band of masterless men it was a startling elevation — and, as Toshizō sees, it forced the break with Itō’s faction, who had deserted their lords precisely so as not to serve one again.

Itō appeals to sokuin no jō, the ‘heart of compassion’ that the philosopher Mencius named as the seed of humaneness — the reflex that makes one start to a child about to fall into a well. Rendered into a warrior’s idiom it becomes bushi no nasake, the mercy a samurai owes a beaten foe: to strike Chōshū while it lies wounded, Itō argues, is to forfeit that, and with it the name of samurai.

ch34.anchor: Sennyū-ji in the eastern hills of Kyoto
ch34.note: Sennyū-ji, in Kyoto’s Higashiyama, had been the mortuary temple of the imperial house since the thirteenth century, the emperors’ graves lying within its grounds; Kaikō-ji is one of its sub-temples. The meeting-place looks ahead: when Itō’s men formally left the Shinsengumi in the spring of 1867 they styled themselves the Goryō-eji, the ‘Guards of the Imperial Tombs,’ nominally charged with tending these very graves (Emperor Kōmei had just been buried here). Historically grounded.

ch34.anchor: but will the wholesaler sell it that cheap?
ch34.note: Shinohara plays on a proverb, sō wa ton’ya ga orosanai — literally ‘the wholesaler won’t let it go at that price,’ meaning ‘it won’t be that easy.’ He then turns the merchant image into the figure that runs through the chapter: Toshizō is the okeya, the cooper, who binds the loose staves of the corps into one tub with hoops no shock can spring. The pun linking the two tradesmen does not survive into English.

ch34.anchor: the man later known as Kirino Toshiaki
ch34.note: Nakamura Hanjirō took the name Kirino Toshiaki after the Restoration. It is a pointed pairing: the Satsuma man-cutter who steers Itō toward the imperial party here would end, like Saigō, in revolt against the very government he helped to make, dying at Shiroyama in 1877.

Hijikata really did keep a book of haiku under the pen-name Hōgyoku; some forty-one verses survive as the Hōgyoku hokku-shū, compiled in the spring of 1863 before he went up to Kyoto and now held at the Hijikata Toshizō Museum in Hino. The preponderance of spring poems, and of plum blossom, is genuine. Corroborated.

Gidayū-bushi, the dramatic sung narration of the puppet theatre and the kabuki stage, named for the chanter Takemoto Gidayū (1651–1714); a taste for it marks Toshizō as a man of the Edo-country townsman’s world, not the schooled samurai’s.

ch34.anchor: that sold saké and sweet saké
ch34.note: The ‘sweet saké’ is amazake, a thick, barely alcoholic drink of fermented rice, served warm and sold at night-stalls; that Toshizō asks for it in place of wine is what draws Shichiri’s sneer, ‘how gentle of you.’

ch34.anchor: he had loosened his blade in its scabbard
ch34.note: To ‘cut the carp’s mouth’ (koiguchi o kiru) is to break the sword free of the tight fit where the guard meets the scabbard mouth — the first motion of a draw. Done idly, with a laugh, it is a silent threat.

A gō-ō pledge-sheet issued by the Kumano shrines, printed over with the crows sacred to their gods; to swear on one and break the oath was held to call down divine punishment. Shichiri’s calling it ‘old-fashioned’ is the joke of a man who no longer quite believes in it.

Yadake, a slender, hard bamboo whose straight canes were cut for arrow-shafts; a warrior household grew a stand of it as both material and emblem. The farm boy’s planting it, in longing to be a samurai, is preserved in the Hijikata family traditions.

ch35.anchor: one plank bridge, with neither railing nor handrail
ch35.note: The bridge at Nijō in those years crossed the Kamo in two spans, resting midstream on a nakasu, a grassy sandbar — the ‘Nijō Nakasu’ of the chapter title. The river has since been narrowed and embanked and the sandbar is gone; the modern Nijō-ōhashi is a single span.

Tenchū, ‘the chastisement of Heaven,’ was the slogan under which loyalist swordsmen in these years murdered officials, merchants, and rival activists, often pinning a placard on the body to justify the killing as a public execution rather than a private one. Kennosuke, below, boasts of just such a tally.

Konnyaku (konjac) is a firm, near-tasteless jelly made from the corm of the devil’s-tongue plant, about as bland a food as a Japanese kitchen offers. ‘A man who will take neither vinegar nor konjac’ is a proverb for one so contrary that nothing whatever will move him.

ch35.anchor: served, too, as a constable's informer
ch35.note: A meakashi: a commoner, very often a reformed gambler or ex-convict, employed off the books by the town constables as a thief-taker and informer. Yohei’s past explains why he can read Toshizō’s trade at a glance and why his blood is up.

Hitokiri, ‘man-cutter’: the era’s word for its political assassins, a handful of whom (Kirino among them, see ch34) became legends. Shichiri claims the title for himself; the boast of a private count of the dead was itself a mark of the type.

ch35.anchor: whipped a tasuki round to bind back his sleeves
ch35.note: A tasuki is a cord looped across the back and over both shoulders to gather the long kimono sleeves out of the way of the arms; a swordsman going into a fight tied one on, here improvised from the sageo, the cord that secures the scabbard at the belt.

ch35.anchor: exposed the head on a stake
ch35.note: Sarashi-kubi: the severed head set on a spike at a public place beside a written placard naming the dead man’s offense. It was the ordinary end the loyalist bands meted out to those they killed, and the fate Toshizō grants he himself only just escaped.

Daikon, the big white radish: as a term of contempt it means a duffer, a nobody — used of a wooden actor or, as here, of a swordsman reckoned no threat. Shichiri had sold Toshizō to his hirelings as an easy kill.

ch36.anchor: a corps banner with the chrysanthemum crest
ch36.note: The sixteen-petalled chrysanthemum is the crest of the imperial house; to fly it was to claim the Court’s own sanction. Itō’s faction left the Shinsengumi on the tenth of the third month of Keiō 3 (14 April 1867), a month after the death of the Emperor Kōmei, and took the commission of Goryō-eji, guards of that emperor’s tomb at Sennyū-ji — the very temple where the plot was hatched (ch34). They based themselves at Kōdai-ji. The dates are historically exact. The breach ran to its end at Aburanokōji in the eleventh month of the same year, where Kondō had Itō killed.

‘Tōshō Daigongen,’ the Great Avatar Shining over the East, was the divine title under which Tokugawa Ieyasu was enshrined at Nikkō after his death in 1616. Kondō’s argument is that the shogun’s office of sei-i taishōgun — ‘great general who quells the barbarians’ — was itself conferred by the Court, so that to serve the shogunate is to serve the Throne; Itō hears in it only a man who has swallowed the shogunate’s case whole.

ch36.anchor: a stray by-blow of Lord Tōdō
ch36.note: Lord Tōdō was the daimyō of Tsu, in Ise. The tale that Heisuke was his unacknowledged son is a tradition attached to him and not established fact; Shiba gives it as legend, and it colors the townsman’s touchiness about being taken for a mere farmer’s recruit.

ch36.anchor: the singing of a hauling-chant in the timber-yards
ch36.note: Kiyari: the rhythmic work-song by which gangs of laborers hauled great timbers or raised heavy weights together, a sound of the Edo townsman’s trades — and, sung by firemen, a mark of the swaggering iki style. Fukagawa, across the river, was Edo’s great lumber district.

ch36.anchor: a May wind blowing clean through his belly
ch36.note: An idiom for an open, uncomplicated, empty-headed nature: as though nothing weighed inside a man but a light spring breeze. That even so breezy a soul as Heisuke had turned to the loyalist cause is Toshizō’s measure of how the times were running.

ch36.anchor: A memoir of that night by Shinohara Tainoshin
ch36.note: Shinohara’s written reminiscences are a genuine source for the split, and Shiba quotes them here (with his own bracketed glosses) in their stiff classical Japanese. That the memoirist boasts of having gone resolved to kill Kondō and Hijikata, and been given no opening, is a self-portrait to weigh accordingly — the loser’s account of a quarrel he lost.

ch36.anchor: killed him outright with a single stroke
ch36.note: The killing of Takeda Kanryōsai by Saitō Hajime on the Takeda road is historical, in the sixth month of 1867; Takeda, drifting toward Satsuma, was cut down as a deserter under the corps law. The scene stands as Kondō and Hijikata’s wordless reply to Itō’s faction. Corroborated.

ch37.anchor: an Edo foot-guard permanently stationed in the city
ch37.note: An okachi was a foot-soldier retainer of the shogun, the lowest rank of direct vassal, who went on foot where mounted men rode; jōfu means his post kept him permanently in Edo rather than rotating to a lord’s home province. Oyuki is thus of low but genuine Edo samurai stock — the source of the crisp, unsoftened Edo speech that so draws Toshizō.

That Satsuma’s two coming giants, Ōkubo and Nakamura Hanjirō (Kirino), personally cultivated Itō’s little band measures how seriously Satsuma took it: not as ideological friends but as a ready-made strike force inside Kyoto, to be spent when the day came. Historically grounded.

ch37.anchor: a captain of a Great-Guard unit
ch37.note: The ōgoban, the Great Guard, was one of the shogunate’s standing military corps of hatamoto. In the sixth month of 1867 the whole Shinsengumi was taken into direct shogunal service and its leaders given Great-Guard rank — Kondō as a unit commander, Hijikata as a captain. For men born to farming families it was a startling rise, and it is the ‘risen in the world’ that Oyuki gently needles him about. Historically accurate.

ch37.anchor: would have looked down on the samurai of the domains
ch37.note: The distinction is between a jikisan or direct retainer of the shogun (see ch33) and a baishin, a ‘rear-vassal’ — the retainer of some daimyō, and so only the shogun’s vassal’s vassal. Even a common Shinsengumi trooper, now a direct retainer, outranked in theory the samurai of the great domains; the lowest of them fell below omemie, the privilege of being received in the shogun’s presence.

Mokuroku, ‘the catalogue,’ was a middle license in a sword school, above the beginner’s kirigami and below full menkyō; it certified that the pupil had been shown the school’s recorded techniques. Toshizō’s doctor-brother had reached it as a boy under Kondō’s adoptive father.

Rai San’yō (1780–1832), poet and historian, whose Nihon Gaishi (see ch30) shaped the loyalist imagination of the age; to write ‘in the manner of San’yō’ is to write Chinese-style verse in his admired, vigorous mode.

Tatami-iwashi: tiny whitebait spread in a lattice and dried into a thin, crackling sheet, toasted and eaten as a relish — a homely Edo food. That Oyuki asks for it, and colors as she does, is the whole of her homesickness in one word, and it is her Edo-ness Toshizō loves.

ch38.anchor: billeted ahead and lodge at the honjin
ch38.note: A honjin was the official inn of a post-station on the great highways, reserved for daimyō, court nobles, and high shogunal officials on their journeys; quarters were booked ahead by billeting-men, and a wooden placard (sekifuda) naming the lodger was hung at the gate. For a farmer’s son to travel so, with a name-board of his own, is the whole comedy of the chapter’s opening.

ch38.anchor: the site of the Naval Drill Ground at Teppōzu
ch38.note: The signs of the opening country were rising in Edo itself: a school for training with foreigners by the Hitotsubashi gate, and, on the old naval ground at Teppōzu (Tsukiji), the Tsukiji Hotel, Japan’s first Western-style hotel, begun in 1867 for the foreign residents the treaties now admitted. Historically grounded.

The Kiheitai, ‘irregular militia,’ was the mixed-class volunteer corps raised in Chōshū by Takasugi Shinsaku in 1863, open to farmers and townsmen alongside samurai; drilled in Western style, it became the backbone of Chōshū’s new army. Toshizō wants the same raw material for the same reason — that men with a stipend to lose no longer fight.

An anpotsu-kago was a heavier, better-appointed palanquin than the open town kind, one that sumptuary custom reserved to samurai households of standing. That Toshizō arrives home in one is exactly the ‘stiff neck’ the Hino folk resent.

Ishida sanyaku, ‘Ishida Powder,’ was a real folk remedy for bruises and sprains compounded by the Hijikata family of Ishida village and hawked from village to village — the trade the boy Toshizō carried on his own back. Koryōsan, ‘consumption powder,’ was another family preparation; that it could do nothing for Okita’s tuberculosis makes Toshizō’s faith in it the more affecting.

ch38.anchor: returned the government to the throne
ch38.note: The Taisei Hōkan: on the fourteenth of the tenth month of Keiō 3 (9 November 1867) the shogun Tokugawa Yoshinobu formally offered to return the governing power to the imperial Court, and it was accepted the next day — ending, on paper, two and a half centuries of Tokugawa rule. Toshizō sets out to recruit for a shogunate that has, unknown to him, just surrendered its authority; the news reaches him only at Odawara. Historically exact.

The phrase renders nishiki o kazaru, ‘to deck oneself in brocade’ — from an old Chinese saying that to win success and not return home to be seen in it is like walking abroad by night in embroidered silk. Hikogorō means that Toshizō owes the home country the sight of his success; Toshizō, characteristically, will not perform it.

ch39.anchor: the eighteenth of the eleventh month, in the third year of Keiō
ch39.note: The Aburanokōji Incident. The lunar date Keiō 3/11/18 converts to 13 December 1867. Kondō lured Itō to his residence, plied him with drink, and had him speared and cut down on his way home near the Aburanokōji; the corps then left the body as bait and ambushed the Goryō-eji who came to recover it, killing Tōdō Heisuke, Hattori Takeo, and Mōnai (Kenmotsu). The novel makes the swordsman who finished Itō one Mutō Katsuzō; other accounts name Ōishi Kuwajirō among the assassins. The sequence of events is well attested.

Sei-i Taishōgun, 'Great General who Subdues the Barbarians,' the full title of which 'shogun' is the everyday abbreviation. First given to commanders sent against the Emishi of the north, it became from the twelfth century the title of the hereditary military ruler of Japan.

Minamoto no Yoritomo (1147–1199), founder of the Kamakura shogunate and the first warrior to rule Japan as Sei-i Taishōgun. Kondō's point is that a warrior house had held real power for the near seven centuries since.

Yoshitsune (1159–1189), Yoritomo's younger half-brother and the most dazzling commander of the Genpei War, hunted to his death by the very brother he had won the war for. He is the proverbial beautiful, doomed, melancholy hero — hence Toshizō's jibe about a chief who broods 'with a pale face like some Yoshitsune.'
Mount Tai (Taizan) in Shandong, foremost of China's five sacred peaks and a stock image for massive, unshakable steadiness.

The Western folding umbrella (kōmori-gasa, 'bat umbrella'), so named for its black ribs and cloth. A novelty of the treaty-port years; that hatamoto and then townsmen were carrying it marks how fast Edo was Westernizing by 1867.

ch39.anchor: There were no fireworks at Ryōgoku this year
ch39.note: The summer fireworks over the Sumida River at Ryōgoku Bridge had been an Edo institution since the 1730s. Their cancellation registers the unsettled, money-short mood of the capital in the last year of the shogunate.

Jōfu: retainers of a domain posted permanently to Edo rather than rotating home under the alternate-attendance system. Their children were Edo-born and Edo-bred, which is why Nagakura's homesickness for the city runs deeper than the others'.

ch39.anchor: he changed his name to Kashitarō to mark it
ch39.note: Itō took the name Kashitarō (甲子太郎) to commemorate the sexagenary year kinoe-ne (1864) in which he joined the Shinsengumi; on defecting to Satsuma he changed it again, to Settsu. The serial renaming, the narrator notes, was peculiarly his own habit.
The Noh play Chikubushima, named for the island shrine of the goddess Benzaiten in Lake Biwa. That Itō is cut off mid-chant lends the killing its theatrical hush.

ch40.anchor: unmoving as a mountain, unhurried as a forest
ch40.note: An echo of Sun Tzu — 'swift as the wind, quiet as the forest, fierce as fire, immovable as the mountain' — the maxim Takeda Shingen bore on his war-banner (fū-rin-ka-zan). It is Toshizō's ideal for the corps, and he quotes another strain of it aloud a few lines on.

Toshizō names the standard reading of a half-schooled samurai: the Analects of Confucius and the Mencius; the Jūhasshiryaku, a Yuan-dynasty digest of Chinese history long used as a Japanese primer; and the Nihon Gaishi, Rai San'yō's popular history of the warrior houses.
The two Chinese classics of war: the Sunzi (Sun Tzu's Art of War) and the Wuzi, ascribed to the general Wu Qi. Toshizō prefers these books of pure tactics to the moralizing histories.

ch40.anchor: the way a bystander reads a game of go
ch40.note: From the proverb okame-hachimoku: the onlooker at a game of go sees eight moves further than the players absorbed in it. Toshizō means that book-learning only sets a man second-guessing his own resolve.

ch40.anchor: on the second day of the fifth month of the thirty-first year of Meiji
ch40.note: That is, 2 May 1898. Yoshinobu (1837–1913) lived out his thirty-year retirement in near-total seclusion and was only then received again by the Emperor Meiji — the measure, for Shiba, of the completeness of his self-effacement.

ch41.anchor: boasted the authority of the Tokugawa
ch41.note: The Fushimi Magistracy (bugyōsho), the shogunate's administrative and judicial seat for the Fushimi post-town and its river port south of Kyoto. Its walled compound made a natural forward strongpoint; the next chapter finds the site built over as a housing estate.

The nine gates (kumon) of the outer enclosure of the Kyoto palace. To be commanded to guard them was to be received back as a trusted Imperial force — a total reversal of Chōshū's disgrace after the Hamaguri Gate affair of 1864, and a sign of how far Satsuma had turned the court.

The Minié rifle, a muzzle-loader firing the expanding conical Minié ball; its rifled barrel gave range and accuracy far beyond the old smoothbore musket. Its spread is the material fact behind Chōshū's transformation in four years.
The 'four-kin' (yonkin) gun, a light rifled field piece throwing roughly a four-pound shell — the modern French-derived artillery of the new-model armies, outranging the shogunal side's smoothbores.
The Geweer (Japanese geberu), a Dutch smoothbore percussion musket without even a rear sight: obsolete beside the rifled Minié, and typical of the shogunal side's mixed, dated equipment.

A married woman of the townsman and samurai classes shaved her eyebrows (and blackened her teeth); unshaved brows mark this woman as keeping the presentation of a maiden or an independent widow rather than a matron. Toshizō is describing Oyuki, a samurai widow.

ch42.anchor: turned again at the Battle of Toba-Fushimi
ch42.note: The Battle of Toba-Fushimi (Keiō 4/1/3–6, i.e. 27–30 January 1868), the opening clash of the Boshin War, fought on the roads into Kyoto from the south. Though heavily outnumbered, the Satsuma-Chōshū forces broke the shogunal army; when the Imperial brocade banner was raised, the Tokugawa side became 'rebels,' and the campaign was decided. Well attested.
The battle of Sekigahara (1600), at which Tokugawa Ieyasu's victory made him master of Japan and founded the order that Toba-Fushimi would bring down.

Matsumoto Ryōjun (1832–1907), later Matsumoto Jun: shogunal physician, pupil of the Dutch doctor Pompe, founder of Japan's first Western hospital at Nagasaki, and after the Restoration the army's first surgeon-general and a baron. Shiba's aside that he opened Japan's first sea-bathing beach is right in substance but wrong in place — the beach was at Ōiso (1885), not Zushi, as the author's own hedge, 'Zushi, I believe,' half-concedes.
J. L. C. Pompe van Meerdervoort (1829–1908), the Dutch naval surgeon who from 1857 gave Japan its first systematic instruction in Western medicine, at Nagasaki.
Hōgen ('Eye of the Law'), in origin a Buddhist clerical rank, was granted by the court as an honorary title to eminent physicians, painters, and other men of skill.

ch42.anchor: the Winter and Summer Sieges of Osaka
ch42.note: The two campaigns of 1614–15 in which Ieyasu manufactured pretexts to destroy the Toyotomi house — reduced by then to a single great domain at Osaka — that his own overlord's heir, Hideyori, still headed. Toshizō sees the same maneuver being worked on the Tokugawa now, and in the same castle.

Mitogaku, the historiography built around the Dai Nihonshi compiled by the Mito Tokugawa, which judged the past by loyalty to the throne and branded the disloyal 'enemies of the Court.' Yoshinobu, a Mito son, could not bear to wear that name — the flaw, Shiba argues, that unmanned him.

The tōsatsu-hyō, the manifesto under which the shogunal army marched on Kyoto, cast as a petition to the throne against the Satsuma 'traitors.' By 'rising to the challenge' with it, the Tokugawa side gave Satsuma exactly the war it wanted.

ch43.anchor: which one might call a second Warring-States age in the nation
ch43.note: 'Boshin' is the sexagenary name of the year 1868 (Keiō 4 / Meiji 1), and the war that opens here is named from it. Shiba's 'second Warring-States age' looks back to the century of sixteenth-century civil war that Ieyasu had ended.
The shirasu, the white-graveled forecourt of a magistracy, where the accused knelt and sentence was pronounced — a fitting seat for the corps that had policed Kyoto by the sword.

The corps' own standard bore the single character makoto ('sincerity'). Over it they now flew the Rising-Sun ensign as the flag of the whole shogunal army, in the conviction that theirs was Japan's lawful government. The claim would collapse within days: once the Imperial brocade banner (nishiki no mihata) was carried over the Satsuma-Chōshū side, the Tokugawa army became, in law, a rebel host.

ch43.anchor: commander of the Fourth Army in the Russo-Japanese War
ch43.note: Nozu Michitsura (1841–1908) rose to field marshal and commanded the Fourth Army against Russia in 1904–05; his elder brother Shizuo, the outpost captain here, also became a general. Shiba's habit of flashing forward to these junior officers' later eminence measures how many of Meiji's commanders were blooded at Toba-Fushimi.

Ōyama Iwao (1842–1916), the young Satsuma gunner on Ryūunji-yama, became army minister, field marshal, and commander-in-chief of the Manchurian armies against Russia — one of the towering figures of the Meiji state.

The Asobi (elsewhere the ju) were the neighborhood bands into which the sons of upper Aizu samurai were grouped from about age six; each afternoon's meeting opened with the recited code Shiba gives here, which in its full form ended with the famous line, 'What must not be done, must not be done.' It bred the ferocious discipline that would make Aizu's stand — and its tragedy — in this war.
The Naganuma-ryū of military science (gungaku), the tradition of tactics and drill in which the Aizu domain trained its troops.

ch43.anchor: the Great Elder of the shogunal council
ch43.note: The tairō ('Great Elder'), the highest office of the shogunate, filled only in a crisis and by custom from a few premier hereditary houses — the Ii of Hikone chief among them, whose Ii Naosuke had held it at the time of the Perry treaties. Their going over to Satsuma is thus a defection of the Tokugawa vanguard itself.

ch43.anchor: became the first shot of the Battle of Toba-Fushimi
ch43.note: The shell from Nozu's Satsuma battery, fired about 5 p.m. on Keiō 4/1/3 (27 January 1868), was indeed the first shot of Toba-Fushimi and so of the Boshin War. Contemporary accounts agree the Satsuma side fired first, a bursting shell throwing the shogunal column into confusion. Well attested.

ch44.note: A thin wood on the western edge of the Fushimi post-town, before the magistrate’s office. It took its name from Shizuki, the low hill in Fushimi where Toyotomi Hideyoshi raised his first Fushimi Castle in the 1590s (the castle was wrecked by an earthquake in 1596 and rebuilt on higher ground nearby). Here the Satsuma and Chōshū riflemen turned the grove into the tatami-walled strongpoint the next lines describe.

ch44.anchor: tatami mats requisitioned from the townhouses
ch44.note: Tatami, the thick rush-faced straw floor-mats of a Japanese house (each roughly 90 by 180 centimeters and several centimeters deep), were dense enough to stop or slow a lead ball. Stacked into a chest-high wall, requisitioned mats gave the Satsuma-Chōshū gunners an improvised bulletproof breastwork — a detail well attested in accounts of the Fushimi fighting.

ch44.anchor: too many of their guns were matchlocks
ch44.note: The hinawajū, a muzzle-loading gun fired by a smoldering cord touched to the priming pan — in essence the weapon the Portuguese had introduced to Japan in 1543. It was slow to load, short-ranged, and useless in rain. By 1868 it was three centuries out of date against the rifled Minié (see the note at chapter 41). That the shogunal side’s Aizu troops were still largely armed with matchlocks, against Satsuma-Chōshū Minié rifles, is the technological gap Shiba is drawing here.

ch44.anchor: Sagawa Kanbei, captain of the Aizu
ch44.note: Sagawa Kanbei (1831–1877), an Aizu senior retainer nicknamed the Oni-Sagawa, the “Aizu ogre,” for his ferocity in the field. He led the han’s Bessentai, its picked bodyguard-and-assault unit, in Kyoto, and fought through Toba-Fushimi and the long defense of Aizu in 1868. He survived the war, entered the new government’s police, and was killed in 1877 leading a police brigade against the Satsuma rebels in the Seinan War. “Special-Selection corps” here renders Bessentai.

The Denshūtai (“training corps”) was the shogunate’s Western-drilled infantry, trained from 1867 by the French Military Mission and armed with modern rifles. Its men followed Ōtori Keisuke (who enters this novel later) north after the fall of Edo and fought on to Hakodate. It was the most modern force on the Tokugawa side, which is why Shiba sets it in the same column as the antique Aizu troops.

ch44.anchor: cut off his head and hang it at their waists
ch44.note: Taking an enemy’s severed head as proof of a kill, to be tallied afterward for reward, was standard practice in the wars of the sixteenth century. On a battlefield swept by rifle fire it was a dangerous anachronism: a man laden with two heads, as the text says, could barely move. Shiba uses the Aizu troops’ head-taking to mark how far their whole way of war had fallen behind the Satsuma-Chōshū riflemen.

ch45.anchor: the British legation secretary Ernest Satow
ch45.note: Ernest Satow (1843–1929), the young British interpreter and diplomat whose fluent Japanese and Satsuma-Chōshū sympathies made him an influential figure in the last Tokugawa years; he served under Minister Sir Harry Parkes. His memoir, quoted here, is A Diplomat in Japan (1921); Shiba cites it from the Japanese translation. Satow’s eyewitness detail — the Fushimi fire seen from Osaka — is genuine, and corroborates the scale of the blaze.

The decisive battle of 1600, in which Tokugawa Ieyasu’s Eastern army crushed the coalition (the “Western army”) loyal to the Toyotomi, opening the way to the Tokugawa shogunate. Shiba’s point is the parallel: at Sekigahara, as at Toba-Fushimi, the numerically stronger side lost for want of will, only a few units fighting in earnest. The comparison frames Toba-Fushimi as the mirror-image undoing of what Sekigahara had built.

In the sixth month of 1867 the Shinsengumi, until then hired swords in Aizu’s pay, were formally taken into direct shogunal service, its officers granted the standing of hatamoto (see the note on hatamoto at chapter 2). This is why Nagakura, a deserter from Matsumae by birth, could now lord it over the recruited “infantry” as their social superior. The “Ōgobangumi” (Great Guard) was one of the shogunate’s standing hatamoto guard corps.

Matsudaira Masatada (1844–1868 in office as commander; d. 1897), daimyo of Ottō and nominal commander-in-chief of the shogunal field army at Toba-Fushimi. “Buzen-no-kami” is a court title, not a personal name. His repeated orders to fall back, relayed here, are historical; the collapse of the shogunal command is a main theme of these chapters.

ch45.anchor: though he had taken three bullets in his body
ch45.note: Hayashi Gonsuke (Yasusada), the old Aizu commissioner of artillery introduced at chapter 43, was mortally wounded directing his guns in the road at Fushimi and died of these wounds during the battle (early February 1868 by the Western calendar). His refusal to be carried to the rear is recorded in Aizu accounts. His son Hayashi Matasaburō, named near the end of this chapter, was killed in the same fighting.

ch45.anchor: the Tōdō clan on the shogunal side
ch45.note: The Tsu domain of the Tōdō house, holding the fortified pass at Yamazaki southwest of Kyoto for the shogunal side, changed sides on the third day and turned its guns on its former allies once the Court had declared Satsuma-Chōshū-Tosa the Imperial army. This defection, opening the shogunal flank, is well attested and was decisive in the rout. There is a bitter irony in the name for readers of this novel: the corpsman Tōdō Heisuke, killed at the Aburanokōji, was of no relation.

ch45.anchor: and this came to the shogunal army swollen in the telling
ch45.note: The nishiki no mihata, the Imperial brocade banner, marked whichever army carried it as the legitimate Imperial force and its enemy as chōteki, rebels against the Throne. Secretly prepared in advance by Ōkubo Toshimichi and Iwakura Tomomi, it was bestowed when Prince Ninnaji-no-miya Yoshiaki was named supreme commander on the fourth day of the First Month (28 January 1868) and raised at the front on the fifth. Its effect was less military than moral: no daimyo wished to be a rebel against the Emperor, and waverers went over or melted away. Shiba makes this — not any defeat in the field — the true breaking of the Tokugawa cause. The banner’s date and effect are well attested; whether its design carried real Imperial sanction from the outset was disputed even at the time.

ch46.note: The sanjikkoku-bune, the long, low passenger boats that plied the Yodo River between Fushimi and Osaka’s Hachikenya landing, rated at a nominal thirty koku of cargo (see the note on koku at chapter 2). They were the ordinary public transport of the route, and here they carry the Shinsengumi’s wounded down from the lost battle.

ch46.anchor: a fortress of metal walls and boiling moats
ch46.note: This renders kinjō-tōchi, a Chinese-derived phrase (“walls of metal, a moat of boiling water”) for an impregnable stronghold. Osaka Castle, raised by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in the 1580s and rebuilt on a vaster scale by the Tokugawa after 1620, was the greatest fortress in the land, sited by the shogunate expressly to hold the western daimyo in check. That Yoshinobu would abandon it without a fight — the subject of the rest of this chapter — is precisely what made his flight so stunning.

ch46.anchor: the Winter and Summer sieges of Osaka
ch46.note: In the winter of 1614 and the summer of 1615 Tokugawa Ieyasu twice besieged Osaka Castle to destroy the Toyotomi house that Hideyoshi had left behind; the castle fell and the Toyotomi were annihilated, sealing Tokugawa supremacy. Sanada Yukimura (Nobushige), the defenders’ most brilliant captain, was killed in the final battle and became the type of the doomed loyal warrior. Shiba’s irony is exact: Toshizō now looks to the same castle for a last stand, but with the sides reversed — it is the Tokugawa cause that is failing.

Inoue Kaoru (1836–1915), known in his Chōshū youth as Inoue Monta; one of the “Chōshū Five” who studied secretly in London. He rose to be a leading Meiji statesman — foreign minister and, as Shiba’s aside notes, a marquis. His analysis quoted here, of how the shogunate might have strangled the thinly-held Imperial position from Osaka, is the counsel of a man who became one of the age’s shrewdest political operators.

ch46.anchor: toward ten at night on the sixth of the First Month
ch46.note: Yoshinobu’s secret flight from Osaka Castle on the night of Keiō 4/1/6 (30 January 1868) is historical fact and the decisive act of the Boshin War’s opening. Abandoning an intact army and an impregnable fortress, he slipped out with a small party — among them Matsudaira Katamori of Aizu and, as the next paragraph notes, Katamori’s brother Matsudaira Sadaaki of Kuwana — boarded an American warship (the USS Iroquois) for the night off Tenpōzan, and at dawn transferred to the shogunal steam warship Kaiyō-maru, which bore him to Edo. His own commanders were not told. With this, the shogunal cause collapsed not in battle but by the desertion of its head.

ch46.anchor: He has left a written account of it
ch46.note: Fukuchi Gen’ichirō, pen-name Ōchi (1841–1906), a shogunal interpreter present in the castle that night who became one of Meiji Japan’s foremost journalists (editor of the Tōkyō Nichi Nichi Shimbun) and a Kabuki playwright. The passage that follows is Shiba’s condensation of Fukuchi’s memoir; the “I” of it is Fukuchi himself.

Enomoto Takeaki (1836–1908), the Dutch-trained commander of the shogunal navy and captain of the Kaiyō-maru, the finest warship in Japanese waters. He refused to surrender the fleet after Edo’s fall, carried the remnant of the Tokugawa forces north, and set up the short-lived republic at Hakodate where this novel will end; pardoned afterward, he became a Meiji cabinet minister. He enters the story here, at the edge of Yoshinobu’s flight, as the man who still commands the ships off Tenpōzan.

ch47.anchor: the historical place of Ashikaga Takauji
ch47.note: Ashikaga Takauji (1305–1358) founded the Muromachi shogunate after breaking with Emperor Go-Daigo and setting up a rival “Northern” emperor, driving Go-Daigo’s “Southern Court” into exile. The Mito school of history — whose monument was the vast Dai Nihon-shi begun under Tokugawa Mitsukuni (1628–1701) — treated the Southern Court as the legitimate line, and so branded Takauji the arch-traitor and exalted his enemy Kusunoki Masashige (see chapter 6), who died for Go-Daigo, as the model loyal subject. By the 1860s this framing was the shared assumption of educated men on every side; it is the exact fear driving the passage — Yoshinobu would sooner desert his army than fight the Emperor’s banner and go down in history as “a second Takauji.” The account here is accurate to how the period understood itself.

ch47.anchor: the newly-appointed infantry captain Matsudaira Tarō
ch47.note: Matsudaira Tarō (1839–1909), a Western-minded shogunal official who would follow Enomoto Takeaki north and become vice-president of the short-lived Ezo republic at Hakodate — the campaign this novel is moving toward, and the “fate” the narrator foreshadows here. He appeared in the previous chapter as the friend who first told Fukuchi of Yoshinobu’s flight.

The Hohei kokoro-e (“Infantry Handbook”), a translation of a Dutch army drill-book of 1860, issued by the shogunate’s military institute. The technical vocabulary Toshizō sounds out — soldaat (private), compagnie (company), onderofficier (non-commissioned officer), korporaal (corporal) — is Dutch, the language through which the shogunate first took in Western military science before the switch to French instruction. That Toshizō, an unlettered farmer’s son, reads a foreign drill-manual with delight while high officials dither is the chapter’s quiet point.

The Fujiyama (Fujisan) was an American-built steam warship of the shogunal navy, among the more modern vessels in Japanese waters. It carried the Osaka remnant, the Shinsengumi included, back to Edo after the collapse at Toba-Fushimi.

In the old twelve-fold reckoning of the day, the Hour of the Ox (ushi no koku) ran roughly from one to three in the morning — the dead of night, chosen here so the corps could slip out of Osaka unobserved.

ch47.anchor: a crested formal coat and Sendai-hira hakama
ch47.note: Toshizō dresses for Oyuki in his best: a montsuki, the black silk coat bearing the family crest worn on formal occasions, over hakama of Sendai-hira, a fine ribbed silk from Sendai long prized as the finest cloth for a man’s formal trousers. For the blunt soldier of the preceding chapters to take such care is the measure of the meeting.

ch48.anchor: a poet named Fujiwara no Ietaka
ch48.note: Fujiwara no Ietaka (1158–1237), one of the great poets of his age and a compiler, under the retired Emperor Go-Toba, of the Shin-Kokin Wakashū (1205), the eighth imperial waka anthology. By tradition he spent his last years on this hill above the sea at Naniwa (old Osaka) practicing nissokan, the “sun-contemplation” — the first of the sixteen meditations of the Contemplation Sutra, in which one gazes at the setting sun to fix the mind on Amida Buddha’s Pure Land in the west. The spot took its name, Yūhigaoka (“Hill of the Evening Sun”), from the practice, and the mound they find is his reputed grave; the death-poem quoted just below is the one attached to him by this tradition.

A gorintō, a stone memorial built in five stacked stones — cube, sphere, pyramid, half-moon, and jewel — for the five elements of Buddhist cosmology (earth, water, fire, wind, and the void). Common as a grave-marker from the Heian and Kamakura periods on, it is the form of Ietaka’s reputed tomb here; the stone is read “Karyū-zuka,” a Sino-Japanese reading of the same characters that spell his name.

Danna-sama, “master” or “husband,” is the deferential word a wife uses for the man of her house. That Toshizō — a bachelor of thirty-four who has never been anyone’s husband — confesses to having dreamed since boyhood of being addressed by this one word, and gently scolds Oyuki the next morning for leaving it off, is the quiet heart of the chapter.

ch49.note: Yamazaki Susumu (died 1868) was a historical member of the Shinsengumi, an Osaka man who joined at the first recruitment and served as a kansatsu (inspector), the corps’s internal watch and intelligence arm. He is bound up above all with the Ikedaya affair of 1864, where by tradition he scouted the loyalist plotters. The Shinsengumi’s own records have him wounded at Toba-Fushimi and dying of the wounds aboard the Fujiyama-maru on the passage east, buried at sea as the novel describes; a few modern historians doubt the shipboard death, but it is the account Shiba follows.

ch49.anchor: the bond of this one meeting
ch49.note: An allusion to ichigo ichie (“one lifetime, one meeting”), a maxim of the tea ceremony holding that every gathering is unrepeatable and must be met as though it will never come again. Toshizō, an amateur of neither wealth nor leisure, reaches for the tearoom’s own idea of impermanence to say that a soldier can promise a woman nothing but the fullness of the present hour.

ch49.anchor: the hushed jakkō-light of the Buddha
ch49.note: Jakkō (寂光, “the light of quiescence”) is a Buddhist term for the serene radiance of enlightenment, and by extension of the Pure Land itself. The wordplay turns on two characters read shō: 照 (a hard, glaring “shining”) and 昭 (a soft “radiance”). The retreat is written Saishō-an with the gentler 昭, and Toshizō reads into it the quiet, valedictory glow of a setting sun rather than a blaze.

ch49.anchor: matsukaze, from Kameya Mutsu in Kyoto
ch49.note: Matsukaze (“wind in the pines”) is a flat, baked confection of wheat flour, malt syrup and white miso, poppy-seeds strewn on its glazed upper face and the underside left plain. It is the signature sweet of Kameya Mutsu, a Kyoto confectioner founded in 1421 that has long supplied the Nishi Hongan-ji temple; by the shop’s tradition the cake began as a siege ration during Oda Nobunaga’s decade-long war on the Ishiyama Hongan-ji (1570s) and took its name from a poem lamenting that hungry time. A Kyoto sweet, then, that carries the memory of a doomed defense: a pointed thing to set before this particular guest.

ch49.anchor: the resolute man never forgets that he may lie in a ditch
ch49.note: Toshizō is quoting Mencius (孟子, “Téng Wéng Gōng II”), who attributes the words to Confucius: the resolute officer never forgets that he may end in a ditch or gully; the brave officer never forgets that he may lose his head. The saying holds that a man of principle accepts from the outset an unhonored death, his corpse thrown in a gully and his severed head passing to the enemy. Its bleak fatalism suits Hijikata’s creed better than Kondō’s wish to be well buried.

Sendai-hira is a heavy, finely woven silk from Sendai, the most prized cloth for a samurai’s formal hakama (the pleated divided skirt). With a crested montsuki jacket it made the gravest ceremonial dress a man could wear; that Kondō rises from his sickbed to put it on marks how much weight he gives the naval funeral.

ch49.anchor: the anchorage off Tenpōzan at Osaka
ch49.note: Tenpōzan is a low artificial hill raised in 1831 from spoil dredged at the mouth of the Aji River, where it enters Osaka Bay; the deep water off it served as Osaka’s outer anchorage for seagoing ships, which could not ascend the shallow river to the city itself.

Shiba’s parenthesis is accurate. After Perry, the shogunate ordered in 1854 that Japanese ships fly the red sun-disc on white to distinguish them from foreign vessels, and used it as its own war-flag through Toba-Fushimi. It was the Restoration government that formally made the Hinomaru the national ensign, by the Commercial Shipping Regulations (Daijōkan Proclamation No. 57) of the first month of Meiji 3 (27 January 1870, old calendar); a separate proclamation that autumn fixed the naval flag. So in the First Month of Keiō 4, when Yamazaki is buried under it, the sun-disc is the shogunate’s flag, not yet by law the country’s.

Shinagawa was the first of the fifty-three post-stations of the Tōkaidō, the great highway between Edo and Kyoto, lying just south of Edo proper at the head of the bay. To come ashore there was, in effect, to arrive at the gate of Edo; it is a fitting first billet for a corps that has fought its way back from the capital it lost.

ch49.anchor: the shogunal Igakusho, the medical school by Izumibashi in Kanda
ch49.note: The Igakusho was the Tokugawa government’s school of Western (Dutch-derived) medicine, grown out of a vaccination clinic and by this date housed near Izumibashi in Kanda, Edo. Its director was Matsumoto Ryōjun, the bluff army-physician who has already tended Kondō and Okita at Osaka; it is to his institution that the two wounded men are carried ahead. It later became a root of the medical faculty of the University of Tokyo.

A kaimaki is a padded, kimono-shaped bedcover with sleeves and a collar, pulled over the sleeper like a wearable quilt; a single thin one, thrown over a man lying down in his clothes, is the barest sort of bedding, and the measure of how little comfort the corps now commands.

ch50.note: Officials of the Edo shogunate were assigned by rank to particular waiting-rooms in the castle, named for their painted screens; the Fuyō (hibiscus) Chamber was the room for a middling tier of office-holders, among them the town magistrates, the finance magistrates, and the administrators of outlying garrisons such as Kōfu. To say a man was “of the Fuyō Chamber” was to fix his standing at a glance.

Kōfu, in Kai province, was tenryō, land held directly by the Tokugawa house rather than granted to a daimyō (the text’s “heaven’s-domain”). Once the domain of the warlord Takeda Shingen, it commanded the mountain approaches to Edo from the west, and the shogunate garrisoned it and administered it through an appointed Kōfu kinban shihai. Its notional yield of a million koku made it the greatest prize lying loose in the collapse.

Itagaki Taisuke (1837–1919) commanded the Tosa contingent of the new government’s Tōsandō (Eastern Mountain Road) column marching on Edo, and it was his force that took Kōfu ahead of the Shinsengumi. He is far better remembered for his later life as the founder of Japan’s Freedom and People’s Rights Movement and the man of the apocryphal cry, “Itagaki may die, but liberty never!”

The shogunate dressed the two farmers’ sons in the ranks of the ruling class before sending them out. A wakadoshiyori (“junior councillor”) was one of the second tier of the shogun’s ministers, an office normally reserved to hereditary daimyō; yoriai-seki was the standing of the highest grade of hatamoto, the direct bannermen. Kondō’s delight (“We’re daimyō”) is the point: titles that would once have been unthinkable for men of their birth were now, with the house in ruins, handed out for the asking. Historically Kondō also took a samurai alias, Ōkubo Yamato, for the campaign.

Danzaemon was the hereditary title of the head of the eta and hinin, the communities the Tokugawa order held to be outcaste, whose leader ruled them from Asakusa in Edo and controlled such trades as leatherwork. In exchange for the men and money he could raise, Kondō had the councillors formally lift the discrimination against his people and enroll Danzaemon himself among the hatamoto; historically this was the thirteenth Danzaemon (Dan Naoki), freed from outcaste status in the first month of 1868. Some hundred of the two hundred men he sent were gunners, and they made up much of the corps’s new strength.

Shiba’s parenthesis is in error: the Minié rifle was a muzzle-loader. Its innovation was the Minié ball, a soft lead bullet with a hollow base that expanded into the rifling when fired, giving a muzzle-loading rifle both long range and a quick reload; it was the standard infantry arm of the 1850s and 1860s and the weapon whose accuracy had cut the Shinsengumi up at Fushimi. True breech-loaders (the Snider, the Spencer) were only then coming into the war, on the new government’s side.

ch50.anchor: a trooper of the Shinchōgumi held in ward by the Shōnai domain
ch50.note: The Shinchōgumi were the Edo remnant of the same 1863 levy of masterless swordsmen that produced the Shinsengumi: the men who went back east rather than stay in Kyoto. By this date they served as a police force under the Shōnai domain (in today’s Yamagata), which is what “held in ward by” denotes. Okita’s brother-in-law being one of them places Okita’s family firmly on the shogunal side.

ch50.anchor: Heigorō, a nurseryman living at Ikebashi-jiri in Sendagaya
ch50.note: This detached wing of a Sendagaya gardener’s house is where Okita Sōji historically spent his last weeks; he died there of consumption at the end of the fifth month of Keiō 4 (1868), a few months after this scene and without ever learning how the war ended. The novel is quietly setting the stage for a death it will not narrate on the battlefield.

ch51.note: The old lord is Yamauchi Yōdō (1827–1872), the retired daimyō of Tosa and one of the “four wise lords” of the Restoration; Geikai Suikō, “the Drunken Lord of the Whale Sea,” was his own literary sobriquet, and here names a record kept in his circle. His parting line to the troops, ten nao samushi, jiai seyo (“the season is yet cold; take care of yourself”), became famous, and Itagaki has it recited to his men again below, where its weight is less the warning than the reminder that they march for their own lord.

The propaganda was real, and it worked. Itagaki Taisuke’s family, the Inui, held a tradition of descent from Itagaki Nobukata, a senior general of Takeda Shingen, the sixteenth-century warlord whose old capital was Kōfu; the family had taken the name Inui generations before after a disgrace. Marching to seize Kai, Itagaki restored the ancestral surname (by most accounts at Ōgaki, as here) and spread word that Shingen’s Imperial descendant was coming home, turning a province of Tokugawa sympathizers toward the new government almost overnight.

ch51.anchor: walking abroad in brocade by night
ch51.note: Kondō’s “Tang saying” is in fact older, from the Records of the Grand Historian: the warlord Xiang Yu, urged to hold the capital, answered that to be rich and honored and not return to one’s home country was “like walking by night in embroidered robes,” with no one to see. It is the perfect motto for a farmer’s son parading a daimyō’s palanquin through the villages he grew up in, and Kondō, who cannot read it in the original, has it exactly right.

A horo was a large cloak of cloth stretched over a light bamboo frame and worn on the back of a mounted warrior; filled by the wind it ballooned into a great bag that could turn a spent arrow and, more to the point, made its wearer conspicuous as a mark of rank. By this date it was purely ceremonial, an antique of the picture-scrolls, which is why Onobu knows it only from warrior-prints; that the shogun’s house should present one to Toshizō measures both the honor and its unreality.

The shoin-bangashira commanded one of the elite guard units of the shogun’s own household, an office of high standing among the direct bannermen. It is the post that carried Toshizō’s yoriai rank and the horo with it. His flat “Risen, is it” is the chapter’s quiet counterweight to Kondō’s delight in the same honors.

ch51.anchor: a manuscript called the Riin Shiwa
ch51.note: The Riin Shiwa (“Fireside Tales from the Hedge’s Shade”) is an actual memoir set down by Satō Jin, grandson of the Hino headman Satō Hikogorō and grandnephew of Toshizō, preserving the household’s recollections of the Shinsengumi men it had known from boyhood. Shiba quotes it directly for the Hino homecoming; the passages of Kondō crossing the garden and Toshizō with the horo are, unusually, eyewitness family record rather than the novelist’s invention.

For the campaign Kondō took a samurai alias, shedding the outlaw name the new government had put a price on; the sources give it variously as Ōkubo Tsuyoshi and, later at Nagareyama, Ōkubo Yamato, the form Shiba uses here. The disguise fooled no one for long: within weeks the government gazette was naming “Ōkubo Yamato (Kondō Isami)” as a chief of rebels.

ch51.anchor: a shogunal unit called the Nappa-tai
ch51.note: The Nappa-tai (“rape-leaf corps”) was a shogunal infantry battalion nicknamed for the drab green of its Western uniforms; it was quartered near Kanagawa on the Tōkaidō. Toshizō’s night ride to beg its help is the measure of how thin the Kōyō Chinbutai had worn: two hundred men at the start, already halved by desertion, hoping to borrow the best part of two thousand.

ch51.anchor: was one Inoue Taisuke, then thirteen
ch51.note: The detail is one of Shiba’s genealogical asides, tying the scene to living descendants. The boy was the nephew of Inoue Genzaburō, the Tama comrade and Sixth-Unit captain killed at the Fushimi magistrate’s office in the first days of the war; left behind here at the Satō house, he survived, and through a marriage into Okita Sōji’s family carried a thread of these men down to a household still at Tachikawa in the writer’s own day.

ch52.note: Kondō signs his recruiting writ with the campaign alias, adding a courtly given name, Masayoshi, to complete the disguise of a shogunal officer. The promise it carries, reward once the Tokugawa fortunes are restored, is the same dream of a Kōshū fief he has been chasing since Edo; issued over a false name to villagers who have never heard of the Shinsengumi, it measures how far the corps has drifted from the sworn brotherhood it began as.

Risei is a bookish, Chinese-derived word for a village head, grander-sounding than the everyday shōya or nanushi the narrator glosses it with. Amemiya reaches for it, along with a warlord ancestor and a claim to bear a surname, to dress a farmer’s standing in samurai dignity, exactly the pretension Kondō himself is living out on a larger scale.

ch52.anchor: This Amemiya Keijirō, at this time
ch52.note: Amemiya Keijirō (1846–1911) was a real man and became a far larger one than this scene suggests. A Kōshū headman’s son, he turned after the Restoration to business, built a steam-powered flour mill at Fukagawa around 1880, and rode a career of bold speculation, tramways, colliery, and above all railways, to a great fortune and the nickname “the railway king of Meiji.” Shiba’s aside, down to the water-pipe graft scandal that briefly jailed him and his death in the forty-fourth year of Meiji, is accurate; the swaggering youth who bolts at the first shell here is the same man.

A shaguma was a great flowing crest of dyed animal hair (yak or bear) worn over a commander’s helmet or cap in the new-government armies, a badge of rank visible across a battlefield. As the next lines set out, the color told the domain: Satsuma black, Chōshū white, Tosa red. Harada can read the enemy from the crest alone before a shot is fired.

The memory is of the aftermath of the Hamaguri Gate affair of 1864: when the Chōshū attack on the palace failed, a band of loyalists withdrew to Tennōzan, the hill above the Yamazaki defile between Kyoto and Osaka, and there the veteran ideologue Maki Izumi and sixteen companions took their own lives rather than be captured. The Shinsengumi, first up the hill, found only the dead. That Nagakura should recall it now, climbing another hill four years later against men riding the tide they once fought, is the chapter’s bitter mirror.

ch52.anchor: the first cannon-shot of the eastern campaign
ch52.note: The action here is the Battle of Katsunuma, also called the Battle of Kashio (柏尾), fought on the sixth day of the third month of Keiō 4 (29 March 1868). Itagaki’s Tosa-led vanguard of the Tōsandō column broke Kondō’s Kōyō Chinbutai in about two hours and drove it back toward Edo. Small as it was, it was the first land battle of the war east of the mountains and the stroke that finished the Shinsengumi as a fighting corps; within days it would disband, and Kondō’s road runs from here to Nagareyama and the execution ground.

ch53.anchor: did not even shave his pate
ch53.note: A samurai kept the front of his head shaved, the sakayaki, as a matter of daily grooming; to let it grow out was a visible sign of penance and withdrawal from affairs, like a Westerner going unshaven in mourning. Yoshinobu, having surrendered the government and shut himself in a sub-temple of the Kanei-ji at Ueno, wore the unshaven look of a man doing penance, the outward form of the “absolute submission” by which he hoped to spare Edo.

ch53.anchor: the Shōgitai was coming into being
ch53.note: The Shōgitai (“Corps to Manifest Righteousness”) was a body of pro-Tokugawa loyalists, many of them shogunal retainers, formed in Edo in early 1868 to resist the surrender their own lord had accepted. They took up position around Yoshinobu at Ueno; in the fifth month of that year the new government destroyed them in a single day’s bombardment, the Battle of Ueno. Their rise here marks how far events had slipped past Yoshinobu’s control.

These were the men who saved Edo. Katsu Kaishū, the shogunate’s naval commissioner, and Yamaoka Tesshū, a swordsman and envoy, negotiated with the new government’s commander Saigō Takamori and brought about the bloodless surrender of Edo Castle that spring, sparing the city the assault fixed for the fifteenth. Shiba passes on the theory, a plausible one, that it was Katsu who contrived to arm the Shinsengumi and send it off to Kōshū, precisely to be rid of the men whose presence in Edo most inflamed the Imperial side.

ch53.anchor: raise a monument to the two men
ch53.note: The monument is real and still stands: the Junsetsu Ryōyū no Hi (“Stone of the Two Heroes Martyred to Duty”) at Takahata Fudō in Hino. Every detail of Shiba’s aside is borne out: the inscription composed by the Sendai Confucian Ōtsuki Bankei, the calligraphy by Matsumoto Jun, the plan begun in the ninth year of Meiji (1876), the seal-script header written at last by Matsudaira Katamori after Yoshinobu could only weep at the names and refused, and the stone finally raised in 1888, held back a decade because a monument honoring men who died against the new government was slow to win permission. The weeping is the point the chapter has been building toward: even the lord who used and abandoned them could not, thirty years on, speak their names dry-eyed.

ch53.anchor: In Shimōsa (Chiba prefecture) it is a rich district
ch53.note: Nagareyama, on the Edo River in Shimōsa northeast of Edo, was a prosperous shogunal-domain town of brewers and merchants. Toshizō chooses it as a mustering ground on the road to the north; the reader who knows the history knows what he does not yet, that within weeks the Imperial columns will close on this camp, and that it is here the road of Kondō and Toshizō finally forks.

ch53.anchor: Aizu was still a powerful counter-force
ch53.note: Aizu (in today’s Fukushima), the domain of Matsudaira Katamori, the former Kyoto Protector, was the domain Satsuma and Chōshū hated above all others and the natural rallying-point of the north. It would become the core of the Northern Alliance and, that autumn, the scene of the war’s most terrible siege. Toshizō’s resolve to reach Aizu, formed here almost alone in the room, sets the course of everything that remains of his life, through the northern campaign to Hakodate.

ch53.anchor: the road I go out by—the spring moon
ch53.note: The verse is an actual hokku of Hijikata Toshizō’s, preserved in his manuscript collection under the poet-name Hōgyoku: kōyō ni / dete yuku michi ya / haru no tsuki, “setting out on official duty, the road, and the spring moon.” The cutting-word ya hangs the traveler between his errand and the moon above it. That he answers Kondō’s request for a poem with this one, on the eve of a last campaign, is the novelist’s quiet touch, not the historian’s.

As Kondō marches under the alias Ōkubo Yamato, Toshizō takes one of his own, Naitō Hayato, the name he will carry through the rest of the war. The two commanders of the disbanded Shinsengumi enter Nagareyama as shogunal officers no one there can name, which is exactly why the disguise will not hold once the Imperial scouts arrive.

ch54.anchor: the quarter of the demon gate
ch54.note: The kimon or “demon gate” is the northeast, the unlucky quarter in Chinese and Japanese geomancy, from which evil influences and misfortune were held to come; a house or a castle was sited with an eye to warding it. Kondō, a farmer’s son with no learning in such things, is uneasy all the same to find his camp lying to the northeast of Edo.

Mirin is a sweet, low-alcohol rice liquor used in cooking; Nagareyama was, and remains, a noted center of its brewing. The great warehouses of sweet mash are Shiba’s explanation for the town’s plague of mosquitoes.

ch54.anchor: A billet-board hung at the entrance
ch54.note: A sekifuda was a wooden placard hung at the gate of a lodging to announce the name and rank of the traveler putting up there, in the manner of an official on progress. By hanging one that read “Ōkubo Yamato,” Toshizō dresses the muster up as the lawful billet of a shogunal officer rather than a rebel camp.

A tsubo is the standard Japanese unit of floor and land area, about 3.3 square meters, the size of two tatami mats laid together. Three thousand tsubo is close to a hectare, or roughly two and a half acres.

ch54.anchor: having already pacified the post-towns of the Tōkaidō
ch54.note: The daisōtokufu, the field headquarters of the new government’s eastern expedition, was nominally under Prince Arisugawa Taruhito as Grand Marshal. Advancing along the Tōkaidō, the coast road up from Kyoto, it had reached Sunpu (modern Shizuoka) by the third month of 1868 and made it the staging point for the march on Edo.

ch54.anchor: reached Itabashi on the thirteenth of the third month
ch54.note: Itabashi was the first post-station on the Nakasendō, the inland highway, just northwest of Edo. Here the new government’s Tōsandō vanguard fixed its main camp; the station also held one of Edo’s execution grounds, a circumstance that will matter to Kondō before the month is out.

Historically Kondō gave himself up on Keiō 4/4/3 (25 April 1868), still passing as the shogunal officer “Ōkubo Yamato,” in the hope of sparing his farmer-levy. He was carried off to the new government’s camp, his true identity was established there, and he was put to death soon after; the manner of it is told in a later chapter.

A bukan was a printed directory of the daimyō and of the shogunate’s own officials, listing each man’s name, crest, stipend, and post. That the name “Ōkubo Yamato” stood in no bukan told Itagaki at once that it was an alias, and that its bearer was traveling under a false shogunal rank.

Sakamoto Ryōma and Nakaoka Shintarō were cut down at the Ōmiya lodging-house in Kyoto in the eleventh month of 1867. The killing is now generally laid to the Kyoto Mimawarigumi under Sasaki Tadasaburō; the Tosa men’s conviction that it was the Shinsengumi’s work, voiced here, was widely held at the time but is not borne out by the later evidence. It fed their hatred of the corps all the same.

ch54.anchor: a man of grave and imposing bearing appeared
ch54.note: The scene that follows is drawn from Satō Gennosuke’s own later account of his interrogation. As with the Hino homecoming of an earlier chapter, Shiba quotes a surviving family recollection directly rather than inventing the exchange.

ch54.anchor: the Rikuentai, the rōnin corps of the Tosa domain
ch54.note: The Rikuentai (“Land Auxiliary Force”) and the Kaientai (“Naval Auxiliary Force”) were the two private companies of Tosa masterless men led, respectively, by Nakaoka Shintarō and Sakamoto Ryōma: the one drilled as a land militia, the other traded and ran ships in the loyalist cause. Both lost their captains in the Ōmiya killing.

ch54.anchor: the great cause and the rightful name
ch54.note: Taigi-meibun is the Confucian principle that binds a man to his rightful lord and to the legitimate order of things, and brands a stand against them as rebellion. Kondō, who has spent the war insisting the Tokugawa cause was the lawful one, now reads the Emperor’s banner as having carried that legitimacy away with it; to fight on would be to die a rebel. It is on this, and not on courage, that he and Toshizō at last divide.

Ōshū is the old name for Mutsu, the great province of the far northeast. Here it stands for the northern domains — Aizu chief among them — still under arms against the new government, and so for the war Toshizō means to go on fighting.

ch55.anchor: later he served the new government as head of the College of Engineering
ch55.note: Ōtori Keisuke (1833–1911) was born the son of a village doctor in Akō, and rose through Dutch and then French military studies to command the shogunate’s Western-drilled infantry. He led the shogunal die-hards north in this campaign, fought on to Hakodate, and after the war built the long official career Shiba lists here: the Imperial College of Engineering, the Peers’ School, the legation to Qing China, the Privy Council, a barony. With Enomoto, he was one of the few leaders of the losing side to prosper under the government that had beaten him.

ch55.anchor: the Ogata Kōan academy in Osaka
ch55.note: Rangaku, “Dutch learning,” was the study of Western science and arts through the Dutch, the one European nation allowed to trade at Nagasaki during the country’s long seclusion. Ogata Kōan’s academy in Osaka, the Tekijuku, was its most famous school; from it came many of the physicians, soldiers, and reformers who carried Western knowledge into the last shogunal decade and on into the Meiji state.

ch55.anchor: Katsu Kaishū and Ōkubo Ichiō above all
ch55.note: Ōkubo Ichiō (1817–1888) was a senior Tokugawa official and, with Katsu Kaishū, a leading voice of the party that chose submission and the peaceful surrender of Edo over a fight to the finish. To such men the Shinsengumi, still spoiling for war inside the capital, were an embarrassment; the money they gave Kondō for the Kōshū expedition was, Shiba suggests here, in part to be rid of them.

Goryō-hei were soldiers raised from the tenryō, the shogunate’s own demesne, the lands it held directly rather than granting them to a daimyō. With the Tokugawa house fallen, these were among the last troops still answering to it.

ch55.anchor: the festival day of the Tōshōgū
ch55.note: The Tōshōgū is the shrine at Nikkō where Tokugawa Ieyasu, deified as the god Toshō-Daigongen, is enshrined; the seventeenth of the fourth month was the anniversary of his death and the shrine’s great festival. To win a battle on that very day struck Ōtori as a portent that Ieyasu’s house would rise again.

ch56.anchor: This was the nineteenth of the fourth month
ch56.note: The storming of Utsunomiya Castle told here fell on Keiō 4/4/19 (about 11 May 1868) and was the high-water mark of the shogunal remnant’s march north. The victory did not hold: the new government’s main force retook the castle four days later, on the twenty-third, and Hijikata was shot in the foot in the defense. The army then fell back toward Nikkō and, in time, Aizu — the long retreat that carries the rest of the novel.

The “hanging ceiling of Utsunomiya” is a favorite of the street storytellers: the tale that Honda Masazumi, lord of the castle, built a chamber with a ceiling rigged to drop and crush the second shogun, Hidetada, as he lodged there on his way back from Nikkō in 1622. The plot (the Utsunomiya Affair, for which Masazumi was disgraced) is now generally thought a later invention, but it made the castle’s name a byword. Toshizō means that he knows the place only from the theater.

ch56.anchor: the strategic part that Kusunoki Masashige had played in the Kenmu Restoration
ch56.note: Kusunoki Masashige (met in an earlier chapter) held the little mountain fort of Chihaya against a huge army of the Kamakura shogunate in 1333, and by tying it down helped bring on the brief imperial restoration of the Kenmu era. To make Nikkō a “Chihaya” was to gamble that a small force in strong mountains could pin the new government in place and rally the wavering lords — the whole strategy on which this campaign rests.

ch56.anchor: what the art of war calls a focal ground
ch56.note: Kuchi, a “focal ground,” is one of the nine kinds of terrain in Sun Tzu: a junction where several roads meet, so that whoever holds it commands the approaches to a whole region. Utsunomiya, where the northern highway and the Nikkō roads cross, is exactly such a place, which is why Toshizō insists on taking it while Ōtori’s bookish caution misses the point.

An akazonae was a crack unit turned out entirely in red-lacquered armor. The most feared were the red troops of the Takeda house of Kai; after Takeda fell, Ieyasu drafted its veterans into the Ii house of Hikone, whose “Red Regiment” then led his vanguard at Sekigahara and at the Osaka sieges. That the Ii, once his fiercest van, now marched against the Tokugawa under the Emperor’s banner is the irony Arima and Kagawa are turning over.

ch56.anchor: one of the Three Houses of the Tokugawa
ch56.note: The gosanke, the “Three Houses,” were the senior cadet branches of the Tokugawa — Owari, Kii, and Mito — from any of which a shogun could be drawn if the main line failed.
