Mito, Kagawa’s old domain, was in doctrine the most fiercely loyalist of the three, which is the barb in the narrator’s aside: a Mito man leading the Emperor’s troops against the house he was bred to serve.

ch57.anchor: called Kyorōsan, which Toshizō had left with him
ch57.note: The Hijikata family, makers of the patent bruise-and-fracture medicine Ishida Powder met early in the book, also sold this Kyorōsan as a cure for consumption. It was worthless against tuberculosis; Toshizō’s flat “It works” is the gift of a friend, not a physician’s prescription, and Okita takes it as such.

ch57.anchor: the Kiku-ichimonji blade Sōji had carried in Kyoto
ch57.note: The Kiku-ichimonji (“chrysanthemum and single line”) was a famous line of swords of the Ichimonji school of Bizen, whose smiths were granted the chrysanthemum crest. That Okita carried so fine a blade is a cherished tradition rather than a documented fact; Shiba keeps it, and lets the dying man clasp it at the last.

ch57.anchor: on Keiō 4, the thirtieth day of the fifth month, in that shed
ch57.note: Okita Sōji died at the Sendagaya nursery on Keiō 4/5/30 (19 July 1868), of the tuberculosis that had wasted him since the Kyoto years; his exact age is uncertain, his birth year being given variously as 1842 or 1844. That he died without ever learning of Kondō’s execution, as the following lines have it, is a much-repeated tradition rather than an established fact, but it fits the circumstances: he lay bedridden and hidden through the very weeks in which Kondō was taken and beheaded.

ch57.anchor: The original is in classical Chinese
ch57.note: The short memorial just quoted was composed in kanbun, formal literary Chinese, long the language of record and epitaph in Japan much as Latin was in Europe. The English here follows its measured, classical cadence.

ch57.anchor: The perpetual-memorial fee was five ryō
ch57.note: An eitai shidō-ryō was a lump sum paid to a temple to endow perpetual memorial services: prayers and offerings kept up on the death-anniversaries, in return for the gift, for as long as the temple stood. Five ryō was a modest endowment; the two hundred yen paid when the stone was rebuilt seventy years later was, as the text notes, a considerable sum for its day.

ch58.anchor: the office of rikugun-bugyō-nami, Assistant Commissioner of the Army
ch58.note: Rikugun-bugyō-nami, “associate Army Commissioner,” was a genuine rank in the late-Tokugawa military hierarchy: the deputy grade of the rikugun-bugyō who oversaw the shogunate’s Western-style army. Toshizō’s firmly documented appointment to this office came a little later, in the Ezo (Hakodate) government of the winter of 1868, where he served under Ōtori as effective vice-minister of the army. Shiba brings the title forward to the Sendai phase; the exact dating here is the novel’s, but the office itself is real.

ch58.anchor: as head of the Ōshū alliance
ch58.note: The Ōuetsu Reppan Dōmei, the league of the domains of Mutsu (Ōshū), Dewa, and Echigo, was formed in the summer of 1868 to resist the new government and shield Aizu. Sendai, its largest member, was the keystone; when Sendai wavered and then submitted in the ninth month, as this chapter shows, the league fell apart, and with it the last hope of a stand on the main island.

Date Masamune (1567–1636), known by his posthumous honorific as Lord Teizan, was the one-eyed warlord who founded the Sendai domain and built its castle at Aoba. The Date house he left was, at 625,000 koku, among the greatest in Japan. Toshizō appeals to the memory of its martial founder to shame the present lord toward war.

ch58.anchor: the artillery officer Brunet, the artillery sergeant Fortant
ch58.note: Jules Brunet (1838–1911) was a French artillery officer of the military mission that had drilled the shogunal army. When France recalled the mission, Brunet resigned his commission and stayed on to fight beside the shogunal remnant, following Enomoto and Hijikata north to Hakodate: the foreign officer who cast his lot with the losing side, and, much later, one of the historical inspirations for the film The Last Samurai.

ch58.anchor: a Shimizu no Jirōchō or a Kunisada Chūji might have said
ch58.note: Shimizu no Jirōchō (1820–1893) and Kunisada Chūji (1810–1851) were famous bakuto, gambler-bosses of the late-Edo underworld whose exploits filled the popular storytellers’ repertoire. To say that Toshizō’s stump-speech sounded like theirs is to set his blunt, plain-man’s eloquence a world below the polished statecraft the moment demanded — the narrator’s affectionate needle.

ch58.anchor: he passed for a brilliant scholar even at the Shōheikō
ch58.note: The Shōheikō (the Shōheizaka Gakumonjo) was the shogunate’s official academy in Edo, the seat of orthodox Confucian learning and the training-ground of its scholar-officials; the modern University of Tokyo counts it among its forerunners, as the next line notes. That the unlettered Toshizō had once bested one of its star pupils sword in hand is just what gives Ōtori’s jab its edge.

ch59.anchor: twenty-six Krupp rifled guns of twelve-centimeter bore
ch59.note: Shiba’s figure is not quite right. The Kaiyō-maru, built for the shogunate at Dordrecht and completed in 1866, carried at her commissioning eighteen Krupp 16-centimeter rifled muzzle-loaders together with eight 30-pounders — twenty-six in the main battery, of thirty-four guns in all. The bore was 16 centimeters, not 12, and not every one of the twenty-six was a Krupp piece; but she was indeed among the most powerful warships afloat in her day.

This is the Second Schleswig War of 1864. Shiba’s own label, the “Denmark–Austria war,” drops Prussia, and it was Prussia — not Austria — that was the dominant partner in the alliance that crushed Denmark; the next paragraph names both powers correctly. Enomoto is traditionally said to have gone to the front as an observer while a student in the Netherlands, though the detail is biographical rather than firmly documented.

ch59.anchor: up for sale at a thousand ryō
ch59.note: By the late Tokugawa the standing of a shogunal retainer had become, in effect, a commodity: an impoverished gokenin or hatamoto family could sell its house rank and stipend to an outsider with money and learning, who thereby bought his way into the samurai class and the shogunate’s service. Enomoto’s father, a commoner’s son and a gifted mathematician, entered the ruling order in just this way.

Inō Tadataka (1745–1818), the shogunate’s great surveyor, who spent the last seventeen years of his life walking the coasts of Japan and produced the first accurate map of the whole country. That Enomoto’s father studied under such men marks the family as serious practitioners of Western-influenced science.

ch60.anchor: one of the few survivors of the Shinsengumi
ch60.note: Ichimura Tetsunosuke (1854–1877) is a historical figure, and the tradition that will pay off the thread begun here is well attested by the Satō family of Hino: in the spring of 1869, shortly before Hijikata’s death at Hakodate, he is held to have sent the boy south out of the doomed fortress carrying his own photograph, a lock of his hair, and a last message to the Satō house of his home country. Ichimura reached them, and it is largely through him and the Satō records that Hijikata’s last years are known. He was killed, as told here, fighting Saigō’s army in 1877.

ch60.anchor: a samurai dies for the man who knows his worth
ch60.note: An old maxim from the Chinese classics — shi wa onore o shiru mono no tame ni shisu — first spoken by the assassin Yu Rang in the Warring States, as recorded in the Zhanguo ce and in Sima Qian’s Shiji: a man of honor gives his life for the one who truly recognizes him. The narrator raises it only to set it aside — Ichimura’s devotion, he says, was something stranger and less reasoned than that.

ch61.anchor: the one domain that held no rice-assessed fief
ch61.note: Almost every daimyō was ranked by the assessed rice yield (kokudaka) of his land. Matsumae, at the far northern reach of Honshū, held territory too cold for rice, and was reckoned instead a castle-holding house with no stated koku figure; its wealth came from its monopoly of trade with the Ainu and the produce of Ezo — fish, kelp, and furs. In this it stood alone among the roughly two hundred and sixty domains.

Shiba’s aside had fallen out of date even as he wrote it. The Matsumae keep he calls a national treasure — the last castle keep raised in Japan in the old feudal style, finished in 1854 — burned down in 1949; a concrete reconstruction was put up on the site in 1961. Today it is the castle grounds and a surviving gate that carry protected status.

Artillery of the period was rated by the weight of its shot in kin (about 600 grams), on the French model then in vogue: a “four-kin” gun threw a shell of roughly four kin, a light field or mountain piece, and the “twelve-kin” cannon that answered it a far heavier one. The kin measure of caliber recurs through these battle chapters.

Here the novel parts from the record. The historical Saitō Hajime did not cross to Ezo: he stayed to fight at Aizu, was interned after its surrender, and never went north at all. Shiba brings him to Hokkaidō in order to write this scene, in which Hijikata saves his life by sending him away. Saitō did live on to the end of Meiji — under the names Yamaguchi and later Fujita Gorō, serving as a Tokyo policeman and ending his days as a school clerk — one of the corps’s last survivors, as the novel says.

ch62.anchor: This ship was later named the Azuma
ch62.note: The ironclad was the former CSS Stonewall, a steam ram built at Bordeaux in 1864 for the Confederacy under the cover name Sphinx. She reached Japan after the American Civil War; the United States, declaring neutrality in the Japanese conflict, held her at Yokohama and would not release her until the fighting was decided, then delivered her to the new Meiji government early in 1869. Renamed Azuma in 1871, she was the first ironclad of the Imperial Japanese Navy, and her coming, as this chapter says, tipped the naval balance against Hakodate.

ch62.anchor: had already been fixed by election
ch62.note: The Ezo regime chose its officers by ballot in December 1868 — a thing without precedent in Japan, where office had always come by birth or appointment. Some eight hundred and fifty-six votes were cast; Enomoto Takeaki was elected president and Matsudaira Tarō vice-president, with Ōtori Keisuke and Arai Ikunosuke over army and navy and Hijikata as assistant army commissioner. Foreign observers, and later writers, often called the short-lived government a republic.

Ōmura Masujirō (1824–1869), a physician’s son of Chōshū turned military scientist, was the architect of the new government’s army and is reckoned a father of the modern Japanese military. His caution here — wait for spring — was overruled. He was cut down by disaffected samurai later in 1869, only months after the events of these chapters.

ch62.anchor: the Tōgō Heihachirō of later days
ch62.note: Tōgō Heihachirō (1848–1934), then an obscure Satsuma gunnery officer, would become the most famous admiral in Japanese history: commander of the Combined Fleet that destroyed the Russian navy at Tsushima in 1905. Shiba, in the midst of a novel of Hijikata, cannot resist the long digression that follows on the young Tōgō aboard the Kasuga — the two men were, for these few weeks, on opposite sides of the same sea.

The wakō were the sea-raiders — mostly Japanese, later of mixed Japanese and Chinese make — who plundered the coasts of Korea and China from the fourteenth to the sixteenth centuries, boarding ships and sacking ports. To the Western-schooled naval officers, Hijikata’s plan to take a modern ironclad by leaping aboard sword in hand seemed a throwback to that piratical past.

ch63.note: This is the Gatling gun, the hand-cranked, multi-barreled forerunner of the machine gun, patented in America in 1862; Shiba’s furigana glosses his “field quick-firing gun” with the name outright. Its rate of fire made it murderous against men crossing an open deck, and in the raid told in the next chapter it would cut the boarders down. Some survivors’ testimony held that the weapon was in truth massed rifle fire rather than a Gatling, but the Gatling account is the standard one.

Kōga (also read Kōka), a district of Ōmi province, was with neighboring Iga one of the two great homes of the ninja tradition — the covert agents and irregular fighters of the warring-states age. That the sober naval officer Kōga Gengo should spring from such stock is a quiet irony the narrator enjoys.

Kuroda Kiyotaka (1840–1900), a Satsuma officer who rose to direct the colonization of Hokkaidō and, in 1888, to become the second prime minister of Japan. His heavy drinking, which the narrator makes the hinge of this comic-tragic scene, dogged his whole career. It was Kuroda who, after Hakodate fell, argued successfully that Enomoto’s life be spared.

ch64.anchor: toward Miyako Bay, the object of the attack
ch64.note: The naval raid on Miyako Bay took place at dawn on Meiji 2/3/25 (6 May 1869). Of the three Ezo-navy ships that set out to seize the government’s ironclad Kōtetsu by boarding, a storm scattered the Takao and the Banryū, and the Kaiten went in alone. Running up under a United States flag, she came alongside bow-first instead of broadside-to; her deck stood some nine feet above the Kōtetsu’s, so the boarders had to drop across one or two at a time and were cut down by the Gatling gun on the ironclad’s deck. The raid failed and the Kaiten escaped back to Hakodate. The episode is well attested in the standard histories of the Boshin War; corroborated.

ch64.anchor: a man had to leap down a full jō
ch64.note: A jō is ten shaku, about 3.03 meters or ten feet — close to the roughly nine-foot difference in deck height that the Western accounts of the battle also record.

ch64.anchor: a piece of three hundred kin
ch64.note: Heavy muzzle-loading guns were rated by the weight of shot they threw, reckoned in kin (a kin being about 600 grams). A “three-hundred-kin gun” thus names a very large piece; the Kōtetsu — the former Confederate ram Stonewall — carried a 300-pounder Armstrong rifle forward, the gun Shiba has in view.

ch64.anchor: forming the shape of the character ri, リ
ch64.note: The images are drawn from the shapes of two kana. To lie リ (ri) is for the two ships to lie parallel, side by side, like that character’s two upright strokes — the position from which every boarder could pour across at once. To lie イ (i) is to meet bow-to-side at an angle, as the Kaiten in fact did, so that the men could cross only one or two at a time.
The cape at the entrance to Miyako Bay, in the Hei district of what is now Iwate prefecture; 閉伊崎 is read here as Heizaki. Miyako lies on the Sanriku coast of northeastern Honshū.

ch64.anchor: There was nothing cowardly in it
ch64.note: Sailing under false colors and striking them for one’s own flag before opening fire was an accepted ruse de guerre in nineteenth-century European naval practice, as Shiba says; to fight on while still under the false flag would have been the breach of custom.

ch65.note: Goyōtō, literally “requisition-robbers,” were bands who plundered under the pretense of levying funds or goods for official — often loyalist — purposes in the disorder of the 1860s. Shiba’s gloss in the text is exact.

The hanseki hōkan, the return of the domain land-and-population registers to the throne. The four leading western lords petitioned to return them in the third month of Meiji 2 (spring 1869), and the court ordered all domains to follow in the sixth month (July 1869); Yūjirō speaks of it here as already accomplished. It was the first step toward the abolition of the domains in 1871. Corroborated, the dating slightly compressed.

ch65.anchor: seemed to be of mixed Ainu blood
ch65.note: The Ainu are the indigenous people of Ezo (Hokkaidō), with a language and customs of their own, distinct from those of the Japanese of the “home islands” (naichi) to the south. The boat-chant and the servant here mark the northern setting.
A yatate is a portable writing-set — a small case holding an ink-soaked wad and a brush, carried at the belt — the pocket pen of its day.

ch65.anchor: Even after Toshizō came to Hokkaidō
ch65.note: Shiba uses the modern name Hokkaidō, an anachronism in these scenes: the island was still called Ezo, and was formally renamed Hokkaidō only in the eighth month of Meiji 2 (September 1869), after Toshizō’s death. The usage is the narrator’s, not the characters’.

ch66.anchor: one photograph of Toshizō now in existence
ch66.note: This is the celebrated seated portrait of Hijikata in Western dress, taken at Hakodate in 1869 — the only known photograph of him, and the source of every later likeness. Carried south by Ichimura Tetsunosuke to the Satō family at Hino, it survives there still. Corroborated.

ch66.anchor: cut some two sun off its end
ch66.note: A sun is about 3.03 centimeters, one-tenth of a shaku; two sun is thus a little over an inch.
Yoshitoyo (義豊) was Hijikata’s imina, or formal personal name, used in a signature such as this in place of the familiar Toshizō. It recurs in his posthumous Buddhist name at the close of the book.

ch66.anchor: at a fishing village called Otobe
ch66.note: The new-government expedition landed on Ezo at Otobe, south of Esashi, on Meiji 2/4/9 (about 20 May 1869), and drove inland toward Hakodate; Esashi and then Matsumae fell in the days that followed. Corroborated.

ch66.anchor: a record-long engagement such as there had never before been
ch66.note: The fighting at the Futamataguchi pass, in the fourth month of Meiji 2 (late May 1869), was one of Hijikata’s few clear successes in the Ezo campaign; his defense there held for many days, until the collapse of the other fronts forced him to withdraw. Shiba’s figures — a sixteen-hour action, thirty-five thousand rounds, a single man lost — are the traditional ones and cannot be checked precisely, but the tenacity of the defense is well attested.

ch67.note: Shōjusan and 203-Meter Hill were the key heights in the Japanese siege of Russian-held Port Arthur in 1904–05, during the Russo-Japanese War, whose capture laid the fortress open — the narrator’s forward glance of some thirty-five years. He goes on to liken Enomoto to the Russian commander Stoessel and Toshizō to Major-General Kondratenko, Port Arthur’s ablest and best-loved defender, whose death in the fighting hastened the surrender.

ch67.anchor: Shinobirika was the one Ainu word
ch67.note: From the Ainu sino pirka, “truly fine” or “truly beautiful.” Shiba gives it as the one Ainu word Toshizō learned in the north; the haiku sets it against the moon over Ezo.

ch67.anchor: Nakajima Saburōsuke was a man who had once been a yoriki
ch67.note: Nakajima Saburōsuke (1821–1869) had been a yoriki, a constable-official, of the Uraga magistracy, and was among those who rowed out to parley when Commodore Perry’s squadron reached Uraga on Kaei 6/6/3 (8 July 1853) — the event that opened Japan. A pioneer of Western naval study, he died with his two sons defending the Chiyogatai battery after the surrender of Goryōkaku. Corroborated.

ch68.anchor: the fifth hour of the night
ch68.note: By the old system of variable hours, the “fifth hour” of the night (itsutsu) fell around eight in the evening.

ch68.anchor: the eleventh of the fifth month of Meiji 2
ch68.note: Hijikata Toshizō was killed on Meiji 2/5/11, which is 20 June 1869 in the Western calendar — not 11 June, a slip that comes of reading the lunar day-number as a Gregorian one. He fell leading a sortie near the Ippongi barrier (Ippongi-kan), on the road between Goryōkaku and the Bentenzaki battery, struck by a rifle-ball while on horseback; the standard account puts the wound low in the back. The exact spot and the identity of the man who fired are debated among historians, and Shiba renders the scene without settling either. Goryōkaku surrendered a week later, on Meiji 2/5/18 (27 June 1869). Corroborated as to date and manner; the particulars remain uncertain.

ch68.anchor: the Gakuheitai of the former Sendai domain
ch68.note: The Gakuheitai was the Western-trained rifle corps of the Sendai domain, reckoned among the best-drilled units to reach Ezo; its commander was Hoshi Juntarō, named here among Toshizō’s supporting officers.

ch68.anchor: there was a small woman who left an offering
ch68.note: Oyuki is Shiba’s invention — he says as much in his afterword — and so is this closing scene at the temple. No such visitor is recorded; the sun-shower and the unnamed mourner are the novelist’s farewell, not a document.
